Matchaya introduces new kakigori dessert series
Image credit: Matchaya
Matcha lovers and tea connoisseurs, you probably already heard of Matchaya . Good news: the beloved homegrown Japanese tea brand is debuting a kakigori series, titled Whimsical Cloud, and here’s everything you need to know.
Matchaya Review: A Dessert Cafe Serving Everything Made Of Matcha
The new lineup will feature five new kakigori creations, AKA traditional Japanese shaved ice desserts.
Image credit: Matchaya
Look forward to creations such as the Signature Koichi Azuki ($22++) , made with single-origin ceremonial matcha, and Burnt Butter Houjicha ($18++) , for a roasted tea flavour.
Image credit: Matchaya
Other highlights: Chocolate Tiramisu ($18++), Strawberry Yoghurt ($20++), and Mango Coconut ($20++), inspired by the iconic mango pomelo sago dessert.
If you’re new to the brand, here are some of their signature drinks: the Koicha Latte ($9.50++) features ceremonial-grade Uji matcha that’s said to be rich and intense in flavour. For something more mellow, the Matcha Latte (from $6.50++) has a more balanced flavour, suitable as a beginner-friendly drink. Image credit: Matchaya
Matchaya also offers a range of mains and desserts. You can enjoy their Signature Matchaya Chicken Katsu ($13++), a rice burger with chicken katsu, matcha mayonnaise, tamago, and lettuce.
Finish your meal with their tea-infused desserts, such as the Signature Matchaya Yuzu ($10++) and Kurogama ($8++), a black sesame rolled cake.
Hop on the matcha trend with these best matcha powder brand s to get you started. If you’re looking for more dessert and coffee spots, here are some of the best cafes in Singapore to visit.

Best Tampines hawker food places
We’ve long heard of the debate on which side of Singapore has the best food. To add fuel to this very entertaining fire, we’ve found 25 hidden Tampines hawker food gems to help East-siders prove their point, in addition to these Tampines cafes .
Whether or not the East side is really the best side, we’ll definitely be willing to travel across the island for these delicious Tampines hawker food stalls.
1. Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge
If you’re looking for delicious old-school bak kut teh, check out Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge , which has an outlet in Tampines. Be sure to order their Teochew-style Pork Ribs Soup ($ 7.50 ) , which features a peppery and porky broth with some succulent ribs. They’re also known for their Mixed Pig’s Organ Fried Porridge ($ 6 ) , a wok hei-laden affair with fresh offal. While you’re here, be sure to try the Large Intestines Braised Mee Sua ($ 6 ) too.
Read our Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge review .
Address: 1 Tampines North Drive, #01-34, T-Space, Singapore 528559
Opening hours: Mon-Thurs 9:30am to 8pm, Fri-Sun 9:30am to 8:30pm
Tel: 9819 7696
Website
Old World Bakuteh & Fried Porridge is not halal-certified.
Old World Bakuteh Review: Teochew Bak Kut Teh With Fried Porridge And Dry Mee Sua At Yishun
2. Ho Yun Tim Sum
Ho Yun Tim Sum is run by an ex-hotel chef from Hong Kong, so you know the dim sum here is legit. Here, crowd favourites include the Prawn Chee Cheong Fun ($3.50) , with silky rice rolls encasing juicy prawns, and a thick, comforting bowl of Century Egg Lean Pork Porridge ($3.50) , all priced under $5. You can also get a basket of deep-fried goodies, with three pieces going for $3.50 , including Carrot Cake ($1.20) a nd Fried Spring Roll ($1) .
Read our Ho Yun Tim Sum review !
Address: Blk 419, Tampines Street 41, #01-80, Singapore 520419
Opening hours: Tue-Sun 5:30am to 3:30pm
Ho Yun Tim Sum is not halal-certified.
Ho Yun Tim Sum Review: Handmade Dim Sum By Ex-Hotel Chef From Hong Kong At Tampines
3. Chai Chee Pork Porridge
Image credit: @ck.sg_food
To warm your tummy, head down to Chai Chee Pork Porridge at Tampines Round Market & Food Centre for some Pork Porridge ($6) , which is said to have a thick, smooth, and creamy texture. For the perfect bite, be sure to pair it with the chunks of crispy you tiao. You can also add an egg at an additional $1 .
If you’re not a fan of pork, you can go for the Chicken Porridge ($6) or Cuttlefish Porridge ($6) too.
Address: 137 Tampines Street 11, #01-39 Round Market & Food Centre, Singapore 522137
Opening hours: Mon-Tue, Thurs-Fri, Sun 6am to 1:30pm, Sat 6:30am to 1:30pm
Website
Chai Chee Pork Porridge is not halal-certified.
4. Nasi Lemak Specialist
Image credit: @lickscreenfortaste
If you’re craving nasi lemak , head down to Nasi Lemak Specialist . Here, a plate of coconut-flavoured basmati rice, served with ikan bilis, peanuts, otah, chicken wing, bergedil, and an egg, for only $6 . Nasi lemak aside, they also have a selection of Malay dishes, including Lontong ($4) and Mee Rebus ($4) .
Address: 137 Tampines Street 11, #01-14, Singapore 521137
Opening hours: Tue-Sat 7:30am to 1pm, Sun 7:30am to 12pm
Tel: 8814 7095
Website
Nasi Lemak Specialist is halal-certified.
5. Fu Yuan Minced Pork Noodle
Image credit: Chan FC on Google Maps
Fu Yuan Teochew Bak Chor Mee will do the trick whenever you need a satisfying bowl of bak chor mee. This hawker food stall occupies a small section of a Tampines kopitiam, and serves Teochew-style BCM with mee pok and handmade dumplings. Teochew Minced Pork Noodle ($5) includes sliced pork, liver, minced meat, meatballs and a full-flavoured soup. Plus, the dish is dressed in an addictive and fiery chilli sauce that has a hint of sweetness to it .
Address: 201C Tampines Street 21, Singapore 523201
Opening hours: Thurs-Tue 5:30am to 1:30pm
Fu Yuan Minced Pork Noodle is not halal-certified.
6. Yummy Sarawak Kolo Mee
Image credit: @monkeymiafoody
Located at Tampines Round Market and Food Centre , Yummy Sarawak Kolo Mee serves some of the finest Sarawak hawker cuisine. They’re known for their signature Sarawak kolo mee, and they also offer wonton mee, spare ribs noodles, and chicken feet noodles.
Their Signature Sarawak Kolo Mee Set Meal (from $6) is topped with generous amounts of fried and boiled wonton, char siew, and thick pieces of tender braised pork. As for the noodles, they are said to be QQ and packed with flavour.
Address: 137 Tampines Street 11, #01-45, Tampines Round Market and Food Centre, Singapore 521137
Opening hours: Sat-Thurs 6am to 2pm
Tel: 9866 2244
Yummy Sarawak Kolo Mee is not halal-certified.
7. Song Han Carrot Cake
Image credit: S W Oon on Google Maps
…

Seoul Garden is letting groups of four pay for three at every Singapore outlet, Sunday to Thursday, until 12 November 2026. Seoul Garden is running it to mark its 43rd anniversary, across the Regular, Premium and Supreme buffet tiers.
Group of four, pay for three runs Sunday to Thursday until 12 November. Photo: Seoul Garden
The diner who eats free is the lowest-priced one in the bill. Everyone at the table has to pick the same tier, and the deal does not run on the eve of a public holiday or on the holiday itself.
How the free seat works
The promotion started on 11 October and runs all day on valid days, from 11.30am to 10.30pm. Aperia Mall keeps shorter hours: 11am to 9.30pm from Monday to Thursday and 11.30am to 9.30pm on Sunday.
Lunch counts too. Seoul Garden applies the deal when student, senior and NSman prices are in play, but the free buffet still goes to the cheapest diner in the transaction, so a table of three adults and one student gets the student’s seat free, not an adult’s.
Deepavali falls on Sunday 8 November this year, with Monday 9 November as the public holiday, which takes both days out of the last week of the promotion.
What each tier costs
Weekday lunch runs 11.30am to 3.59pm, Monday to Friday. An adult pays S$24.90++ for Regular, S$33.90++ for Premium and S$47.90++ for Supreme. Students, seniors and NSmen pay S$15.90++ for Regular and S$24.90++ for Premium. Children aged five to 12 pay S$12.45++, S$16.95++ or S$23.95++ by tier.
Weekday dinner from 4pm and the weekend buffet are priced the same: S$34.90++ for Regular, S$39.90++ for Premium and S$47.90++ for Supreme, with children at S$17.45++, S$19.95++ and S$23.95++. Children under five eat free at any time.
The Supreme adult price is the same at lunch, dinner and weekends.
Wagyu rump is a Supreme tier item. Photo: Seoul Garden
Late nights and the Supreme add-ons
Separately, the Late Night Buffet is back from Monday to Thursday, from 8.30pm, at S$27.90++ for the Regular spread of more than 100 grill and hotpot items. Premium is an extra S$5++, and last seating is at 9.45pm.
Supreme is where the newer items sit. Wagyu rump, cut in thicker strips than the usual thin-sliced wagyu, is on the Supreme tier only, at every buffet outlet. Salmon sashimi is also a Supreme item, at all outlets except Clementi Mall and HarbourFront. Snow crab legs are sold a la carte, from S$5.90++ for Supreme diners.
The anniversary deal ends on Thursday 12 November, and Seoul Garden takes table reservations online.
summary: Seoul Garden's 43rd anniversary deal makes the lowest-priced diner at a table of four free, Sunday to Thursday at all Singapore outlets until 12 November 2026, on Regular, Premium and Supreme buffets.
title: Seoul Garden lets groups of four pay for three, Sunday to Thursday, until 12 November

Penang is getting Malaysia’s first InterContinental resort this December , and it’s trading city bustle for beachfront bliss.
Credit – InterContinental Penang Resort
Set along the quieter shores of Teluk Bahang, InterContinental Penang Resort is a 5-star retreat framed by the Andaman Sea and lush tropical rainforest, bringing 348 rooms and suites , 4 restaurants and bars , an infinity pool and a wellness village to the island’s northern coast.
Credit – InterContinental Penang Resort
The resort’s 348 rooms and suites draw inspiration from Penang’s coastal landscape, with natural textures woven into their designs.
Those looking to make their stay extra special can check out the Sky Terrace Suites , which feature private terraces overlooking the sea, or the duplex Straits Suite , complete with spacious living areas and a rooftop sky terrace.
Credit – InterContinental Penang Resort
Foodies will have plenty to look forward to, with multiple restaurants and bars serving up distinct culinary experiences.
Sulam Restaurant celebrates Penang’s food heritage with local favourites and Peranakan classics, alongside international dishes. Paradiso takes an Italian approach with handmade pasta, artisanal pizzas and regional specialities prepared around a live-fire oven.
Meanwhile, Shinka pairs Japanese culinary techniques with Peruvian influences, while Coastal Restaurant & Bar serves seafood, seasonal dishes and cocktails right by the beach.
Credit – InterContinental Penang Resort
Beyond the dining scene, guests can unwind at Gemala Spa & Wellness Village , take a dip in the infinity pool or squeeze in a workout at the fitness centre. For a more exclusive stay, Club InterContinental offers private lounge access, curated culinary presentations and personalised service throughout the day.
There’s plenty to explore beyond the resort, too. Its Teluk Bahang location puts guests within reach of Penang National Park , Tropical Spice Garden , Entopia and ESCAPE Penang . Those keen to venture further can head to Balik Pulau for a taste of rural island life and, during the right season, its famous durian orchards.
Credit – InterContinental Penang Resort
InterContinental Penang Resort opens just in time for the year-end holiday season. If a quieter side of Penang, complete with beachfront sunsets , good food and nature escapes, sounds like your kind of getaway, keep an eye out for its opening dates and room bookings.
JB’s famous Red House reopens with a century-old biscuit shop from Ipoh & Nanyang cafe
summary: InterContinental Penang Resort opens in December 2026 at Teluk Bahang, introducing Malaysia’s first InterContinental resort with 348 rooms and suites, four restaurants and bars, an infinity pool and a wellness village. Suited to travellers seeking a quieter coastal escape, it combines Penang and international dining with spa facilities and access to nearby nature attractions, making it a useful option for year-end holidays away from the busier parts of the island.
title: Malaysia’s 1st InterContinental Resort opens in Penang this Dec with sea-view rooms & wellness village

body:
Biblophiles, writers, and anyone with their nose in the literary scene would be familiar with the Singapore Writers Festival 2026 . Organised by Arts House Group, this annual multilingual literary festival is easily one of the most anticipated events on the cultural calendar. But, news flash: it is not just an event for readers and writers!
Held from 13 to 22 November 2026, this year’s edition, ‘Hidden in Plain Sight’, spotlights local and international literary stars, such as Amitav Ghosh, Jemimah Wei, Silvia Moreno-Garcia, and Balli Kaur Jaswal. It also includes experiences for everyone and anyone. We’re talking about literary walking tours, performances, film screenings, translation-focused programmes, crime and mystery events, and activities tailored for the little ones. No matter what your current hyperfixation is, there’s a programme at the Singapore Writers Festival 2026 for you.
What to attend at SWF 2026 based on your current hyperfixation
1. If you love true crime, suspense and mysteries:
In line with this year’s festival theme of looking beneath the surface in an era of shifting narratives, there are plenty of fascinating conversations to be had – one of which being crime and mystery. This is for those who constantly find yourselves down the rabbit hole of true-crime documentaries and unsolved mysteries.
Photography: Arts House Group
Save the date on 14 November for Truth on Trial: Fighting to be Heard . This panel discussion brings together writers and storytellers Shiori Ito, Mysara Aljaru and Ken Kwek for a conversation on how difficult truths are uncovered, communicated and contested.
Another highlight is The Making of a Serial Killer panel on 14 November, where authors Seo Mi-ae, Rueben Dass and Jocelyn Suarez swap notes on the process of creating monsters that their readers are genuinely terrified of.
Are mystery genres your thing? Here’s your chance to write your own at Shuffle & Draw: The Mystery Writing Game , where a story is formed when you just pick five cards from a deck of Old Maid cards. Who is the Old Maid and what is she hiding?
2. If you’re curious about the future:
Do rapid changes and thoughts of the future intrigue you more than they scare you? Here are some conversations and masterclasses that might be up your alley.
Award-winning journalist Stephen Witt takes the spotlight on 13 November with his keynote talk, The Thinking Machine , where he unpacks the story behind Jensen Huang and Nvidia. Drawing from a story of obsession and risk, this keynote talk dives deep into the man who laid bets on the AI revolution.
Photography: Arts House Group
Next, Amitav Ghosh takes the stage on 14 November for A Writer’s Reimagining of Our Planetary Future keynote talk. Taking a leaf from his recent works, he questions what the future state of the planet looks like, especially with the slew of catastrophic imaginings.
Come 22 November, renowned sociologist and MacArthur fellow Ruha Benjamin pulls back the curtain on the hidden biases shaping our digital world. At her Ctrl + Alt + Rethink keynote talk, expect to be challenged to question existing systems and dream up better ones.
3. If stories of family, belonging, and things unsaid hit close to home:
Sometimes the words left unsaid, emotional baggage and family secrets speak the loudest. These programmes explore tender conversations that feel difficult, but are worth having.
Mark your calendar on 13 November for Saving Face: Community, Culture and The Unspoken . The programme starts with performative readings by three playwrights and directors – Aswani Aswath, Othman M. Yusof and Ang Xiao Ting – before a panel discussion on how inherited cultural values shape our understanding of the world. Buckle up for a multicultural dialogue on themes that are not openly discussed within our communities.
Photography: Arts House Group
What responsibilities does a writer have when they’re writing about other people’s stories? Writing the Lives at Home discusses exactly this with authors Teo Yeo Yenn and Liang Hong, who’ll be sharing about the power of personal stories, and what it means to write their stories with honesty and care.
On 15 November, author Khin Myint is also set for an intimate conversation on Family, Pain and (Un)belonging . Drawing from his acclaimed memoir that explores family, identity and sense of belonging, he answers thought-provoking questions about his powerful work and shares his personal reflections.
4. If you’re a parent who wants enriching quality time with your little ones:
With a range of family-friendly programmes designed to spark imagination, creativity and a love for stories, kids are more than welcome to join the fun at the Singapore Writers Festival 2026.
Bring the young ones along for Roll, Sing & Sign on 15 November, where they can lend their voices to this interactive singalong with sign language. Come ready for a multilingual adventure that will feature beloved childhood soundtracks like Old MacDonald.
…
summary: Biblophiles, writers, and anyone with their nose in the literary scene would be familiar with the Singapore Writers Festival 2026. Organised by Arts House Group, this annual multilingual literary festival is easily one of the most anticipated events on the cultural calendar. But, news flash: it is not just an event for readers and writers!
title: Singapore Writers Festival 2026: Programmes to bookmark based on your current hyperfixation

It’s hard not to feel left out watching our friends eating and describing the numbing sensation that is Mala . Which is why Makan Malah at Our Tampines Hub help us alleviate that FOMO feeling. With their new outlet that opened on 14 Oct 2026 , diners who have never tried mala xiang guo get to have a taste without any pork or lard .
Credit – Makan Malah via Google
Some of you might be familiar with their founding brand, A Hot Hideout. A highly-rated chain known for its collagen-rich soup base that satisfies the soul. Makan Malah’s first outlet was located at NUS UTown , featuring the same level of satisfaction. Also, Makan Malah has announced on their Instagram that they’re in the process of receiving their Halal certification . Do check now and then to see if they receive it.
Credit – Makan Malah via Google
If you have ordered mala before, you’ll know it is very similar to ordering yong tau foo. Pick out the ingredients of your choosing from their freezer; I love enoki mushrooms with a burning passion, and just pass it to the staff at the front. They will then have it weighed. Based on the NUS outlet, the ingredients cost S$2.98 per 100g . Lastly, you can choose between a stir-fry and a collagen soup base.
Credit – Google
Also, they have add-ons, including coriander, peanuts and a peanut sesame sauce. For those, I recommend pairing it with the collagen soup for a more even spread of flavour. Makan Malah also serves beef, something A Hot Hideout does not. They also seem to specialise in more fried items like fried lotus root and potato chips. Other than that, you can expect a traditional mala experience.
Credit – Makan Malah via Google
The restaurant itself is located nearby Tampines MRT with a bus stop, Our Tampines Hub , close by. It is an 8-minute walk from the MRT. Our Tampines Hub is known for a variety of cuisines from all over the world, so what’s 1 more? Give Makan Malah a try, whether you want to experience it for the first time or are just looking for a nice lunch spot.
Shi Xiang Ge: Trust the mala braised meat noodles to impress
summary: Makan Malah is a mala xiang guo restaurant at Our Tampines Hub that opened on 14 Oct 2026, serving a version made without pork or lard. Diners pick ingredients from a freezer to be weighed and cooked as a stir-fry or in collagen soup, with beef and fried items on the menu. It is not yet halal-certified, but suits mala newcomers and anyone near Tampines MRT looking for lunch.
title: Makan Malah – New build-your-own mala with a mouth-numbing kick at Our Tampines Hub

body: The Place If you love your bakes like us, you would probably have learnt that Marymount Bakehouse has opened their newest outlet at Upper Thomson last month. Occupying a corner shophouse space just steps away from Upper Thomson MRT exit on the Thomson-East Coast Line (TEL), this is the bakery café second outlet after their Farrer Park space, and it is a much more spacious outlet with a wider menu as well. The sourdough-focused bakery café is helmed by founder, baker and cook Ian Ferdinand Chong who started out as a home baker. Other than indoor seats, there is also an outdoor terrace which can be pleasant if the weather is forgiving. The Food The new outlet features a sourdough-centered menu that includes handmade sourdough pastas, pies, focaccias, loaves and sourdough-crusted proteins along with expanded brunch offerings and seasonal specials. For a start, I had the refreshing Parma & Burratina Panzanella (S$27) which is a panzanella affair with tomato-watermelon gazpacho confit cherry tomatoes and burratina along with housemade sourdough croutons in 100% extra virgin oil. I also had their Corn & Crab Chowder Pie (4 Inch – S$20.50) where sweet crab meat is folded into a rich corn chowder filling

Singapore does fine dining across the whole spectrum: French precision at Les Amis and Odette, local produce reimagined at Labyrinth, and even vegetable-forward tasting menus at Jag. Here are the best fine dining restaurants in Singapore suited for any occasion. Chasing one cuisine? We’ve got dedicated guides to Japanese , Korean , French , Chinese and Indian restaurants, too.
Oh, and if you’re mapping out your food adventures, don’t miss our guides on romantic restaurants in Singapore or the best restaurants in Singapore .
Why trust this guide
Singapore’s fine dining scene is constantly evolving, and finding the right table is about more than Michelin stars. Our team curates this guide to help you discover standout dining experiences, from celebrated tasting menus to creative kitchens putting their spin on global cuisines. We look at what makes each restaurant special, so you can find the perfect spot for a memorable date night, a milestone celebration or an indulgent night out.
Best fine dining restaurants in Singapore
Here are our recommendations if you’re looking for a sweet fine dining spot:
• Special-occasion splurge: Odette , Les Amis , Zen
• Best tasting menu value: Restaurant Labyrinth , Restaurant Jag
• Elevated flavours: Nae:um , Thevar
• Dinner with gorgeous views: Jaan by Kirk Westaway , Monti , Yan Ting
1. Jiang-Nan Chun
Photography: Jiang-Nan Chun
Take a seat at Jiang-Nan Chun, one of Singapore’s premier Cantonese dining destinations. This Michelin-selected restaurant at Four Seasons Hotel Singapore beckons with a luxurious menu featuring handcrafted dim sum, nourishing double-boiled soups and elevated Cantonese dishes. With Chinese executive chef Alan Chan at the helm, look forward to time-honoured culinary techniques and dishes that are elevated by seasonal ingredients and modern flair. The sophisticated setting completes the luxe experience. Decked out in intricate carved panels and latticework, richly stained wood accents and exquisite leather chairs, the interiors elegantly embody the Jiang Nan region of China.
Let yourself indulge with the curated set lunches and tasting menus. Or, feast a la carte-style with the signature mesquite wood-roasted Peking Duck served with caviar, honey-glazed iberico pork, wok-fried A5 wagyu beef with black pepper sauce, and other standouts. The double-boiled soups are also unmissable, featuring premium ingredients like fish maw, sea whelk and conpoy.
On weekends, explore the refreshed Taste of Hong Kong menu, where chef Alan pays tribute to his Hong Kong roots through classic dim sum, comforting noodles and traditional Cantonese favourites with a modern twist. To top off your feast, raise your glasses to the extensive wine programme.
Planning for an intimate gathering? Book one of the four private dining rooms that sit up to eight to 12 guests, or take advantage of the combined private dining space with a capacity of up to 22 guests. Be it business lunches, family reunions or milestone celebrations, this restaurant does it all.
Best for: Authentic Cantonese cuisine in a sophisticated setting
Michelin stars: One star
Must-try items: Signature Jiang-Nan Chun Peking duck; honey-glazed iberico pork; wok-fried A5 wagyu beef with black pepper sauce
How much: Set lunch from $68 per pax; chef’s signature menu at $238 per pax; a la carte items from $8
Dress code: Smart casual (long pants and close-toed shoes required for gentlemen)
Opening hours: Daily, 11.30am to 2pm & 6pm to 10pm
Address: Level 2, Four Seasons Hotel Singapore, 190 Orchard Boulevard, Singapore 248646
Visit Jiang-Nan Chun
2. Zen
Photography: Zen via Facebook
If you’re in the mood for Swedish fine dining in Singapore, this restaurant comes highly recommended. Occupying a three-storey shophouse on Bukit Pasoh Road, Zen offers exquisite dishes that marry premium European ingredients and Japanese influences. Dining here is a uniquely physical experience: amuse-bouche and aperitifs are served on the first floor before guests head up for the main courses. You’ll cap off the night with desserts at the third level.
Best for: A multi-storey Swedish-Japanese culinary journey
Michelin stars: Three stars
Must-try dishes: Fixed course menu
How much: Lunch set menu from $450++ per pax; dinner set menu from $620++ per pax
Dress code: Smart and elegant or smart casual
Opening hours: Tuesdays to Saturdays, 12pm to 5pm & 7pm to 10.30pm
Address: 41 Bukit Pasoh Road, Singapore 089855
Visit Zen Reserve a table
3. Cloudstreet
Photography: Cloudstreet via Facebook
…

Chinatown Singapore food guide
Chinatown is packed with legendary eats, so it can sometimes be hard to work your way through them all. If you’re struggling to decide, here are the best Chinatown food spots that are definitely worth a visit the next time you’re in the area.
1. Poh Guan Cake House
Poh Guan Cake House is a traditional bakery doling up handmade pastries since the 1930s. One of our favourites was the Yam Biscuit ($1.90) , baked fresh to achieve that golden, flaky crust and creamy paste within. The most popular item, though, has got to be the tau sar piah available in Sweet Green Bean ($1.70) and Salty Green Bean ($1.70) . Each piece crumbled upon being torn in half, and was packed with mung beans for the former, and fried shallots for the latter.
Read our Poh Guan Cake House feature .
Address: 531 Upper Cross Street, #01-57, Hong Lim Complex, 050531
Opening hours: Daily 8am to 7pm
Tel: 6534 0136
Poh Guan Cake House is not halal-certified.
2. You Fu Fried Hokkien Prawn Noodle
Fans of hokkien mee would know of You Fu Fried Hokkien Prawn Noodle , a popular stall with loyal customers who return time and time again for their wok hei-infused noodles. Here, a plate of Hokkien mee is available in three different price points, at $5 , $7 , and $9 , depending on the portion size. You can also add more ingredients to your liking, such as a Stir Fried Egg ($0.70) and more noodles for an extra $1 .
Read our You Fu Fried Hokkien Prawn Noodle feature .
Address: 335 Smith Street, Chinatown Complex, #02-186, Singapore 050335
Opening hours: Mon -Sat 10am to 8pm
You Fu Fried Hokkien Prawn Noodle is not halal-certified.
3. Calendar Coffee
Image credit: Calendar Coffee via Google Maps
Calendar Coffee is a charming cafe only a two-minute walk from Maxwell MRT Station. Opened by the same team behind June Coffee, the cafe offers a range of unique drinks and brunch mains. One of their crowd favourites is the French toast series, with flavours including Apple Pie ($11++) and Smoked Salmon Cream Cheese ($14++) .
Signature drinks include Roasted Rice Latte ($9++) , Jasmine Apple Americano (8.50++) , Miso Caramel Hojicha ($9++) , and the popular Osmanthus Mochi Matcha ($9.50++) : matcha, milk, osmanthus honey, and soft, slurpable milk mochi
Read our Calendar Coffee feature .
Address : 258 South Bridge Road, #01-01, Singapore 058807
Opening hours: Tue-Sun 11am to 6pm
Website
Calendar Coffee is not halal-certified.
4. Heng Kee Curry Chicken Bee Hoon Mee
Tucked away at Hong Lim Food Centre , Heng Kee Curry Chicken Bee Hoon Mee uses a three-generation-old family recipe that’s been constantly refined until today, resulting in a loyal customer base that keeps coming back for more.
Their Curry Chicken Noodle ($7) is good comfort food, with their tasty broth accompanied by large pieces of chicken breast, making for a hearty combination. For those craving a larger portion, their $9.50 version has a bigger serving, together with the option to choose your favourite chicken parts too.
Read our Heng Kee Curry Chicken review .
Address: 531A Upper Cross Street, #01-58, Hong Lim Food Centre, Singapore 510531
Opening hours: Mon-Sat 10:30am to 3:30pm
Website
Heng Kee Curry Chicken Bee Hoon Mee is not halal-certified.
5. Famous Sungei Road Trishaw Laksa
With many accolades to its name, most notably the Michelin Bib Gourmand from 2016 to 2020, Famous Sungei Road Trishaw Laksa is a popular spot among tourists and locals alike. Located at Hong Lim Food Centre , the stall offers two dishes: Fruit Juice Mee Siam ($6) and Asia Delight Laksa ($7) . Both their noodle soups are rich and fragrant without being too jelak, and are topped with an impressive variety of ingredients.
Read our Famous Sungei Road Trishaw Laksa review .
Address: 531A Upper Cross Street, #02-66, Hong Lim Food Centre, Singapore 051531
Opening hours: Mon-Sat 9am to 3pm
Tel: 9750 8326
Famous Sungei Road Trishaw Laksa is not halal-certified.
6. Tang Kay Kee Fish Head Bee Hoon
Hawker stall Tang Kay Kee ‘s modern lunch concept at Hong Lim Food Centre serves up delicious rice bowls that are hearty yet affordable. An all-time favourite is their Pork Fried Rice (from $7) , topped with Black Bean Paste ($1) and Additional Veg ($1) . There are noodle dishes as well, such as the Kong Style Stir Fry Noodles (from $8.50) and Hor Fun (from $6) , made with a mix of ingredients, including fish, prawns, pork slices, and pig liver.
Read our Tang Kay Kee review .
Address: 531A Upper Cross Street, #01-70, Hong Lim Food Centre, Singapore 051531
Opening hours: Mon 11am to 3pm, Tue-Fri 11am to 2:30pm, 5pm to 9:30pm, Sat 5pm to 9:30pm, Sun 4:30pm to 9:30pm
Tel: 8157 2641
Website
Tang Kay Kee Fish Head Bee Hoon is not halal-certified.
7. Ah Heng Curry Chicken Bee Hoon Mee

Halloween falls on 31 Oct, which is a Sat in 2026. With Singapore having plenty of ways to celebrate the season, there’s no excuse not to dress up, round up your friends and spend the night getting spooked.
Instead of staying at home and watching a scary movie , you can take the opportunity to explore Singapore’s various Halloween events. Without further ado, here are 11 best Halloween events in Singapore for a spooky night out.
How I chose these best Halloween events
These are the 3 main criteria I used to decide which events to recommend:
• Variety : The activities on this list cater to a range of interests, from kid-friendly activities to more adult-oriented ones.
• Wide price range : From paid events to free events, there’s something for everyone.
• Strong Halloween theme : I included events known for their immersive Halloween atmosphere.
I have also grouped them into 3 different categories, so you can find what suits you best.
• Neighbourhood trick-or-treat
• Parties
• Events
This isn’t a ranked best-to-worst events list, but a collection of the most enjoyable activities overall, in no particular order.

— Neighbourhood trick-or-treat —
1. Neighbourhood Halloween Parties & Trick-or-Treating
You don’t need to splurge on big-ticket Halloween attractions or events to get into the spooky spirit. Singapore has plenty of neighbourhood Halloween parties closer to home. Community clubs and Resident Networks’ organise Halloween events around our island during the season. Plus, because the events are held around neighbourhoods, most of them are kid-friendly.
You can expect evenings filled with games, crafts and sweet treats at these events. There might also be costume contests, spooky activities and more too. Some events even have haunted mazes, haunted houses and the likes for extra more spooky fun. Use the onePA website to browse community events near you. Do note that some of the events are ticketed, with varying prices, while others have free entry. Do make sure to double-check against the website before heading down to the event, in case it requires a ticket.
For a full list of locations, opening hours & ticket prices, refer here .
Facebook | Instagram | Website
2. Woodgrove Estate: Trick-or-treat (31 Oct 2026)
If you want the upbeat atmosphere neighbouring Halloween events give but amplified, try visiting Woodgrove Estate’s free Trick or Treat event on 31 Oct 2026 . Started in 2007, the 30 residents of this bustling neighbourhood wanted to introduce Halloween to Singapore. More specifically, the tradition of trick-or-treating and other festivities.
Because of this, the streets of Woodgrove Estate in Woodlands transform overnight with impressive decorations and props. Many people also flock here yearly, dressed up in eye-catching costumes. You can really see the kampong spirit in action as they embrace visitors by welcoming them into their estate and providing treats. Be sure to keep your eyes peeled the whole night, as many houses have decorations that’ll leave your mouth gaping open because of how elaborate and intricate they are. Do note that this is a private residential estate after all, so do remain respectful to the residents and fellow visitors.

With options across Woodlands, Bukit Timah, Orchard, Sentosa and other locations, including free community events and ticketed experiences from S$6, the selection suits families, groups of friends and adults seeking different levels of fright and spending.

It seems like everyone and their mother has an Apple Watch these days. And perhaps, you’ve seen a few other similar products and wondered, “What’s the difference?”
Well, we asked ourselves the same question and decided to do a comparison of some of the most common wearable devices ! Here is what we found.
Smartwatches
Credit: Apple
Now, whether you choose smartwatches, smart rings, or fitness bands depends on factors such as what you want to track, how you like to wear your device, and your budget. Let’s first discuss our increasingly common smartwatches .
This is for those of you who like the idea of having a screen on your wrist, where you can get quick information without pulling out your phone. The latest Apple Watches , Samsung Galaxy Watches , and Garmin smartwatches are all compelling options, but which you go for depends mostly on the “ecosystem” you are in, and how deep you are.
Apple Watch Series 12
Credit: Apple
The Apple Watch Series 12 is one of Apple’s latest smartwatches, released in September 2026. iPhone users and those who are very comfortable with Apple devices should definitely consider this as one of their main smartwatch options.
Besides the usual features of tracking workouts and sleep patterns , this latest Apple Watch has other new tricks worth mentioning. A new Health Sensing System provides users with the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.
watchOS 27 brings an upgraded Siri AI to the Apple Watch Series 12, allowing you to get real-world information and have conversations with your virtual assistant anytime. A new Readiness score derived from all your health and fitness statistics also helps you decide how much to push yourself each day.
The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at S$599 , while its more powerful cousin, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 , is available from S$1,199 .
Apple Watch Series 12
Instagram | Website
Samsung Galaxy Watch9
Credit: Samsung
For all the Android users, especially those in the Samsung ecosystem, here’s your alternative. The Samsung Galaxy Watch9 is the latest in Samsung’s smartwatch line, alongside the Galaxy Watch Ultra2 .
Its goal is to be the ultimate everyday health companion for wellness-conscious users. The design is lightweight yet durable , with the Galaxy Watch’s signature cushion silhouette. Pair it with a soft-touch band, and you’ll have a comfortable wearable you won’t mind keeping on all day.
Main features of the Galaxy Watch9 include actionable health insights, activity tracking, and sleep monitoring. Advanced features such as Sleep Apnea , Vitals , and Daily Cardio Load also help to optimise your sleep and training routines.
The Galaxy Watch9 is available from S$518 .
Samsung Galaxy Watch9
Facebook | Instagram | Website
Garmin Venu 4
Credit: Garmin
Honestly, it’s tough to recommend one specific Garmin smartwatch as there are so many. Each model is built with a specific user in mind. The large Garmin smartwatch range includes Outdoor Watches, Running Watches, Diving Watches, Golf Watches, and more.
If you’re an enthusiast in a particular sport or activity, it is likely that you will find your best smartwatch within Garmin’s product range. You can find the Garmin watch for you here .
However, for the sake of this article, we will recommend the Garmin Venu 4 , which is comparable in features to the smartwatches we’ve mentioned so far. If you’re just looking for an everyday watch you can bring on workouts , regardless of your ecosystem, this is worth checking out.
It is also worth mentioning that the Garmin Venu 4 has more than 80 fitness apps , Garmin Coach training plans , up to 12 days of battery life , an LED flashlight , and many more features.
If you’re interested, take a look at the Garmin Venu 4 here , starting at S$729 .
Garmin Venu 4
Facebook | Instagram | Website
Smart rings
Credit: Oura Ring
Let’s talk about smart rings next. These are for those of you who prefer a discreet wearable that blends in as an accessory with your overall fashion choices. Or perhaps you want something less intrusive or distracting, and that feels “invisible”.
If you are someone who checks your stats only once or twice at the start and end of the day, and don’t mind trading quick access to information for a sleek wearable, smart rings might suit you best.
Oura Ring 5
Credit: Oura Ring
Want more than 50 health metrics at your fingertips, literally? Oura Ring 5 gives you that while also being the world’s smallest smart ring. To access information about sleep , activity , stress levels , and more, you will need the Oura app , which is compatible with both iOS and Android .
Note that only basic daily scores and information will be available unless you have an Oura Membership. To get all detailed insights , you need an active subscription, which will cost USD6.99 per month or USD79 per year .
…
summary: What’s the difference between smartwatches, smart rings and fitness bands? We compared prices and features.
title: Smart Wearables 2026: The difference between watches, rings and bands

BTS The City Arirang in Singapore
If you were among the 144,000-plus fans stuck in digital queues during BTS’ June 2026 concert pre-sales, only to walk away empty-handed, we feel you. Between platform glitches and scalpers snatching tickets, getting a seat at the group’s Singapore shows was practically a survival game.
But before you resign yourself to streaming Dynamite and My Universe from your bedroom, we have some good news. BTS The City Arirang is making its 1st and only stop in Southeast Asia right here in Singapore in December 2026 , bringing a month-long lineup of BTS-themed activities and events across the city.
What is BTS The City Arirang?
Image credit: @bts.bigihtoffcial via Instagram
A city-wide fan experience organised by HYBE, the group’s management company, BTS The City Arirang transforms different parts of a host city into a BTS “playground” . This includes installations, light shows, interactive activities, and special events inspired by the group’s music and ongoing ARIRANG world tour.
Image credit: @lynleessweetlife via Instagram
The experience debuted in Seoul in March 2026 before travelling to 4 other cities: Las Vegas, Busan, London, and New York. Along the way, it has illuminated iconic landmarks such as Lotte World Tower, the Empire State Building, and the London Arirang Eye with BTS-inspired displays.
What to expect from BTS The City Arirang in Singapore
Image credit: Singapore Tourism Board
In collaboration with the Singapore Tourism Board (STB), Singapore is next in line to get the BTS treatment, with BTS The City Arirang set to take over the city from 1st to 31st December 2026 .
This will run alongside the group’s highly anticipated concerts at the National Stadium on 17th, 19th, 20th, and 22nd December, marking BTS’s 1st performances in Singapore in 7 years.
With plenty of activities to build up the excitement ahead of the concerts, here’s what to expect at the various activations across Singapore:
Marvel at light shows & illuminated landmarks
Image adapted from: Stefania Guglielmo via Facebook, @singaporetimes via Instagram
Singapore’s iconic attractions are getting a BTS-inspired makeover this December. Jewel Changi Airport’s Rain Vortex will host a themed light and music show , while the National Museum of Singapore will feature light and sound installations inspired by the group’s music.
Image credit: Benny Saik via Facebook
The city’s skyline will get in on the action too, with spots around Marina Bay and the Singapore River glowing red each night from 8th to 22nd December , in tribute to ARIRANG’s signature colour.
These include the Singapore Flyer , Gardens by the Bay , The Fullerton Hotel Singapore , The Helix Bridge , and Anderson Bridge , alongside Millenia Tower , OUE Bayfront , and The Ritz-Carlton , Millenia Singapore .
Immerse in art & multimedia experiences inspired by BTS
Image credit: Exploria via Google Maps
BTS’s music is stepping beyond your AirPods and into the world of art, with themed installations set to pop up across Singapore.
Mandai Wildlife Reserve’s new immersive multimedia experience, Exploria , will get a BTS-themed takeover, while National Gallery Singapore will pair the group’s music with artworks from Pop After Pop: Art Around Us for a dedicated art trail .
Over at Sentosa , fans can look forward to BTS-inspired installations .
Participate in BTS-themed entertainment & activities
Image credit: @universalstudiossingapore via Instagram
For those looking to do more than snap a few pictures, the experience offers plenty of entertainment and activities.
At Sentosa , fans can get moving with a BTS-themed race , while Universal Studios Singapore will put on a fireworks display choreographed to BTS’s music , alongside more special experiences.
The Kallang will also feature interactive activities across multiple activity zones .
Party the night away to your favourite BTS hits
Image credit: Zouk Singapore via Facebook
ARMYs can keep the party going long after the sun goes down at Zouk Singapore , one of the city’s most iconic clubbing destinations. The venue will host opening and closing night events , complete with dedicated music and programming .
Sentosa will also turn up the volume with a rave and drone show set to BTS’s music, so consider this your cue to brush up on your song catalogue and get ready to sing your heart out.
Soak up the BTS fever with BTS The City Arirang in SG
Missed out on tickets to all 4 shows? December isn’t a write-off just yet.
With a month of BTS-inspired light shows, art trails and music-filled events lined up across the island, there are still plenty of ways to get your ARMY fix. STB will be releasing more details in due course, so keep your eyes peeled for updates!

Thye Moh Chan’s Teochew Festival opens at the Chinatown Point Indoor Atrium on Monday, 26 October and runs to Sunday, 1 November, with whole Teochew braised ducks at S$68.80 and halves at S$38.80 on pre-order for collection at the event.
Thye Moh Chan’s Teochew Festival banner. Photo: Thye Moh Chan
Where and when
The festival takes over the Indoor Atrium of Chinatown Point at 133 New Bridge Road. Thye Moh Chan’s permanent shop is in the same mall at #01-45, on 6604 8858. The bakery, part of BreadTalk Group, also has shops at Jewel Changi, Jurong Point, NEX and Paragon.
The braised duck
The duck is slow-cooked for more than six hours and comes with a braised sauce made for it. It is sold on pre-order only. Orders must go in at least two days before the collection date, on thyemohchan.com or by phone on 9479 2294, and collection is only at the festival atrium between 11am and 2pm or 4pm and 7pm. Cash, NETS, Visa and Mastercard are accepted.
Teochew braised duck is on pre-order for collection at the festival. Photo: Thye Moh Chan
Kueh, rolls and tea
New this year is ping pong kueh, a chewy rice-skin kueh filled with roasted peanuts and sesame. A traditional Teochew yam roll costs S$8.80, or S$16 for two, and mung bean cake is S$6.80 for six pieces.
Handmade bo bee kueh, filled with chives, and boxes of three Teochew kueh are S$8.80. Teochew bak chang is S$8.80 each or S$10 for two. Two new drinks, a fingered citron Phoenix Dancong tea and a yam “duck shit” oolong milk tea, are S$6.80 a cup.
Whole and half duck prices. Photo: Thye Moh Chan
Tau sar piah and lanterns
The bakery, which has made Teochew pastries since 1943, is selling its tau sar piah at S$10.80 for a box of eight during the festival. Customers who spend at least S$38 at the atrium can make a mini Teochew lantern for free, limited to one per customer while supplies last.
Corporate orders of more than 50 boxes go to corporate.tmc@breadtalk.com.
summary: Thye Moh Chan's Teochew Festival runs 26 October to 1 November at Chinatown Point, with braised duck from S$38.80 on pre-order for collection at the atrium.
title: Thye Moh Chan brings Teochew Festival to Chinatown Point from 26 October

Skippy Has Blind Box Plushies In 5 Designs, You Can Win A Giant Bean Bag Too

At supermarkets, the socks come bundled with the jar, so there’s nothing to redeem at the counter.

Just pick up the bundle and head to the cashier. The bundles are available at selected Cold Storage, FairPrice, Giant, and Sheng Siong outlets.

Ng Kuan Chilli Pan Mee is opening in Tampines
Image credit: @ngkuanchillipanmee
Easties who are always on the hunt for late-night supper spots will soon have a new go-to. Ng Kuan Chilli Pan Mee is opening its fifth location at Century Square in mid-November 2026— shoppers at the mall have already spotted its hoarding next to popular Taiwanese restaurant Abundance .
Tampines 1 Food Guide: 12 Places For Warabimochi, Famous HK Teppanyaki And More
While opening hours for Ng Kuan’s new branch are yet to be announced, their other outlets are known to open late into the night or even 24 hours, making it an ideal spot for night owls. Beyond that, the store’s Malaysian-style pan mee is loved for its punchy, bold flavours.
You can get their Signature Ban Mian with soup ($6.50) or as a bowl of dry noodles for $6.80 . Each dish comes with al dente noodles, minced pork, ikan billis, fried shallots, garlic, a runny egg, and the star ingredient—hae-bee-infused chilli.
You can also choose from four types of noodles: mee sua, mee hoon kueh, you mian, and ban mian.
For a heartier option, you can add more protein with the Chicken Cutlet , Fish Cutlet , or Pork Cutlet ban mian at $8.80 each .
Alternatively, if you’re after something lighter, consider the Lala Soup ($6.80) , Spinach Soup with Noodles ($7.80) , or just a plain Spinach Soup ($6.80) .
For groups who love to share, there is also a huge selection of sides, including Boiled Lala with Garlic and Chilli ($6.80) , Spinach with Homemade Chilli Sauce ($6.80) , and even Deep-Fried Squid Tentacles ($10) .
If you’re a ban mian fan, read our list of best ban mian in Singapore for $2.50 noodles, abalone mee hoon kueh and more. While you’re in the East, check out our Tampines mall food guide , which will show you the best eats.

Town Restaurant at The Fullerton Hotel Singapore is serving a Hong Kong dinner buffet with dishes created with a chef from its sister hotel in Hong Kong, until Saturday, 31 October. The From Hong Kong, with Love buffet costs S$98 per adult from Tuesday to Thursday and S$118 on Fridays and Saturdays.
The Hong Kong spread at Town Restaurant. Photo: The Fullerton Hotel Singapore
The Hong Kong menu
The guest dishes come from Chef Joy Lui, sous chef at The Fullerton Ocean Park Hotel Hong Kong, and sit alongside Town Restaurant’s regular Treasures of the Sea seafood buffet. The Hong Kong dishes are:
• Cold marinated sea whelk, and chilled jellyfish with scallion oil
• Fried stuffed trio
• Satay beef noodle and curry fish balls
• Braised beef brisket with white radish
• Typhoon shelter prawns
• Hong Kong-style baked pork chop rice
• Lap cheong and pork belly claypot rice
• Egg waffles made to order
• Mango pomelo sago and double-skin milk pudding
• Hong Kong iced milk tea with red bean and grass jelly
The regular seafood buffet runs alongside. Photo: The Fullerton Hotel Singapore
The seafood on ice includes Boston lobster, snow crab legs, half-shell scallops, sea prawns, green mussels and Babylon snails.
Weekend barbecue
On Fridays and Saturdays an alfresco charcoal barbecue adds half-shell scallops with yuzu mentaiko bearnaise, sambal stingray with tamarind and calamansi, and barbecued prawn skewers with a citrus glaze. Sides include duck fat roasted sweet potato, wok-fried baby kailan and confit garlic mash.
Town Restaurant. Photo: The Fullerton Hotel Singapore
Town Restaurant’s alfresco terrace by the Singapore River. Photo: The Fullerton Hotel Singapore
Prices and times
• Tuesday to Thursday, 6.30pm to 10pm: S$98 per adult, S$49 per child aged six to 11
• Friday and Saturday, 6.30pm to 10pm: S$118 per adult, S$59 per child aged six to 11
Prices are subject to service charge and prevailing taxes. The menu may change without notice. The buffet runs until 31 October.
summary: Town Restaurant at The Fullerton Hotel Singapore runs a Hong Kong dinner buffet with Chef Joy Lui until 31 October, from S$98 per adult.
title: Fullerton’s Town Restaurant serves Hong Kong buffet until 31 October

Centro, the restaurant on Level 5 of Shaw Theatres Lido, is opening two hours earlier on weekends. From Saturday 24 October, it opens at 10am on Saturdays, Sundays, eves of public holidays and public holidays for a new weekend brunch menu, served till 2pm. Its usual opening time is noon.
The dining room has floor-to-ceiling windows looking out over Orchard Road. The menu takes its cue from contemporary Australian cafe cooking, with fresh produce and bright flavours.
The Level 5 dining room at Shaw Theatres Lido. Photo: Centro
Savoury plates
The chef’s pick is the Harajuku Savoury Waffle ($22): a vegetable waffle stacked with a poached egg, Brussels sprouts kimchi, pickled ginger and spring onion, finished with bonito flakes and Kewpie mayonnaise.
The Potato, Onion and Rosemary Rosti ($25) comes topped with smoked salmon, crème fraîche, poached eggs, salmon roe and chives. The vegetarian Centro Shakshouka ($22) simmers tomato, onion and housemade red pepper harissa with butterbeans, cannellini beans and spinach, topped with labneh and a poached egg, with grilled pita on the side.
Harajuku Savoury Waffle ($22) from the new weekend brunch menu. Photo: Centro
Other options include Eggs Florentine on an English muffin ($22), a Pastrami and Corned Beef Hash with caramelised onions and toasted brioche ($24), and a vegetarian Cacio e Pepe spaghetti with pecorino, black pepper and a poached egg ($22). Sides include avocado, sautéed mushrooms, and extra smoked salmon or pastrami.
Sweet plates and drinks
Swedish Pancakes ($20) are folded with lemon curd, mascarpone, homemade marmalade and orange segments, served with a small jug of saffron orange sauce. Grilled Homemade Banana Bread ($14) comes with whipped maple butter and salted caramel sauce, and a lighter bowl brings blueberries, banana, candied pecans and Greek yoghurt.
Swedish Pancakes ($20) with lemon curd and mascarpone. Photo: Centro
Coffee is from Toby’s Estate, including a Salted Caramel Popcorn Latte ($7), with matcha from Matcha Project such as the Pomelo Oat Iced Matcha Latte ($7). Brunch cocktails start at $18, among them the Moneypenny Mimosa and Casablanca Bloody Mary, and the Curtain Call mocktail is $14. Free-flow prosecco is $60++ per person for 90 minutes.
No movie ticket needed
Centro is open to everyone, so a cinema ticket is not required to eat there. Shaw Theatres Lido is a few steps away for anyone planning a film after brunch.
Brunch hours: Saturdays, Sundays, eves of public holidays and public holidays, 10am to 2pm. Level 5, Shaw Theatres Lido, Orchard Road.
Source: Centro .
summary: From 24 October, Centro on Level 5 of Shaw Theatres Lido opens at 10am on weekends and public holidays for a new brunch menu served till 2pm.
title: Centro at Shaw Theatres Lido starts weekend brunch from 24 October

body:
Located at Kukoh 21 Food Centre , The $2.50 Shop is a Muslim -owned stall that features over 14 dishes, with everything on the menu going for just S$2.50 each .
Run by 40-year-old Hani Isnin-Racine and her parents, both in their 70s, the trio has been operating this brand for slightly over 2 years. Prior to this, they operated another stall at the same location, offering similar dishes at higher prices.
“We started the S$2.50 meals initiative to help lessen the burden of the vulnerable community (single parents and senior folks who aren’t working due to chronic illness or disability),” Hani shared.
To be ready for their 4.30am (i’m in dreamland at this hour) opening, they arrive at 2am to begin preparations. When asked why they open so early, Hani explained, “We cater to older folks with different sleep patterns due to medication, or those needing to visit the kidney dialysis centre to ‘ chope ‘ good seats for their session.”
What I tried at The $2.50 Shop
With so many choices, I needed a good 5 minutes to decide what to get. After much deliberation, I got the ball rolling with the Nasi Rawon (S$2.50) , with an option to have it either with Cuttlefish or Paru (beef lung).
I chose the latter, and the mound of rice was topped with a generous serving of serundeng , accompanied by sambal goreng , half a bergedil , a bowl of beef stock, and sambal belacan . For its price point, the ingredients were definitely generous.
The beef stock was rich and complex, filled with a few beef chunks. Each spoonful of gravy over the rice was a burst of flavours; a rave party in my mouth.
Hani shared that her mum prepares the sambal belacan fresh daily, using small kampung chilli padi that’s thoroughly washed and deseeded. It delivered a powerful spice kick that jolted my taste buds, waking me up even before my morning coffee— hot but shiok !
I’ve tried paru at several other stalls, and it has always been the same— dry and slightly tough. Thankfully, the version here was soft and moist.
Next, we tried the Lontong (S$2.50) . The rice cake pieces were doused in a thick creamy gravy with a mixture of braised cabbage, long beans and carrots, served with spiced grated coconut and a dollop of nasi lemak sambal .
The pieces of lontong were pillowy, melting in my mouth with ease, and the veggies were braised to a perfect softness.
The gravy had mellow, sweet notes and was prepared with seniors in mind, using a 50/50 blend of pure coconut milk and low-fat milk to keep it low in cholesterol. It was lighter and didn’t feel too jelak , even after many spoonfuls.
The sambal egg was a nice touch. According to Hani’s mum, Mdm Mai, the sambal is cooked for at least 6 hours, with constant skimming of the chilli oil that’s accumulated at the top.
We still had room and gave the Mee Goreng (S$2.50) a try. The stir-fried yellow noods had bits of crab stick, cubes of tau kwa , tau geh , a piece of onion omelette, sambal , then garnished with ku chye , fried shallots and half a calamansi.
To add some brightness, I squeezed in some calamansi juice— hello burst of citrusy goodness!
After mixing the noodles with the sambal , each bite started with a fiery kick that lingered briefly before it faded, leaving only a gentle numbness on your tongue.
There was also a large slab of onion omelette in it— just look at the size! How can this plate cost only S$2.50 ?!
The stall also has a variety of handmade Kueh – Kueh (S$0.80 for 1 , S$2 for 4) . There’s goreng pisang and epok epok , too. The Kueh Kodok Pisang was a moist and fragrant banana ball of deliciousness. My only gripe? Certain parts were slightly dark, resulting in a mild bitterness.
I also tried the Ondeh Ondeh , Kueh Kosui and Kueh Sago . All of them were decent, coated with shredded coconut.
Final thoughts
By the time you’ve reached this paragraph, you’re probably wondering, “Do they actually make a profit?”
Hani was very honest and added, “No, we don’t. There are many monthly bills to settle besides rent and utilities. But despite these sacrifices, it’s worth it when we can help ease the daily lives of the elderly.”
If you’re thinking of swinging by The $2.50 Shop, be sure to check their Facebook page. Hani’s mum’s health has deteriorated since she suffered a minor fracture at work last October— wishing you a speedy recovery!
Let’s support these 3 beautiful, kind-hearted souls. I have the utmost respect for them and am honoured to have made their acquaintance.
People also read :
Which mee siam spots in Singapore are recommended?
Which halal buffets in Singapore are worth a try?
summary: The $2.50 Shop at Kukoh 21 Food Centre serves more than 14 Muslim-owned stall dishes at S$2.50 each, including nasi rawon, lontong and mee goreng, alongside handmade kueh from S$0.80. Open from 4.30am, the family-run stall caters to seniors and budget-conscious diners, with affordable meals prepared to support vulnerable members of the community.
title: The $2.50 Shop: Family-run hawker stall with $2.50 nasi rawon, lontong & $0.80 handmade kueh, opens at 4.30am

Best bowling alleys in Singapore
Even though sports may not be up some of our alleys, bowling is an activity that anyone can participate in and enjoy, especially for those of us who constantly shun the sun or cannot live without aircon.
If you want to get off your butts and burn some calories without breaking too much of a sweat, bowling is the perfect compromise between a fun group activity and a super intense workout at the gym. Here are some affordable bowling alleys in Singapore you can visit with your friends and family for a ball of a time.
1. Planet Bowl
Affordable hourly rates from $14/hour for members
Image credit: Joe Walker via Google Maps
For those of us looking for an affordable leisure activity to spend precious Saturday afternoons at, you can enjoy cheap rates at Planet Bowl for as low as $14/hour if you’re a current civil servant who has signed up for their membership.
For public officers and HomeTeamNS members, lanes start at $18/hour , whereas for the general public, lanes start at $20/hour .
This cosy 20-lane facility has been noted by visitors to be well-maintained, so you are sure to enjoy some quality bowling right here. The staff can also help you set up bumper lanes for kids and beginners to the sport, so you won’t spend your entire session hitting gutter balls.
Rates: From $14/hour for members | $18/hour for public officers and HomeTeamNS members | $20/hour for public
Number of lanes: 20

The Istana Open House Singapore is one of those local experiences in the city that everyone needs to attend at least once, whether you’re here for a holiday or looking to immerse yourself in local culture. The Istana Open House dates can be a little elusive, usually announced quietly, weeks before the actual date. But fret not! We’ve got a list of potential dates to keep your eye on, and all the activities to look forward to, so you know how to spend your time there. There are also plenty of other historical places in Singapore to check out, while you’re at it!
Psst: due to the haze in Singapore , the Istana Open House will not proceed if the PSI exceeds 200, so keep your eyes peeled for updates closer to the date.
Istana Open House Singapore 2026: Details at a glance
Best for: Families who just moved to Singapore; visitors holidaying in the city; history buffs who want to get an inside look at the President’s living quarters
When: 1 November 2026, 8.30am to 6pm
Price (for Singaporeans and Permanent Residents): Free, including accompanying domestic helpers
Price (for foreign visitors): Tickets start from $20; $10 for children between four to 12 years old; free for children under four years old
Opening hours: Only open during the Istana Open House, 8.30am to 6pm
Address: The Istana , Orchard Road, Singapore 238823
Upcoming Istana Open House 2026 dates
The Istana Park decorated for National Day. Photography: Choo Yut Shing via Flickr
The Istana is open to the public up to five times a year. While dates can be sporadic, a good rule of thumb is that it typically hosts an open house in conjunction with a statutory holiday.
Chinese New Year: 22 February 2026
Hari Raya Aidilfitri: March 2026
Labour Day: May 2026
National Day: 26 July 2026
Deepavali: 1 November 2026
Tips before visiting
Photography: The Istana
Pack light and deliberately: There will be security checks at the Istana Open House. Sharp objects, flammable items, tripods, and any metal aerosol, food, or drink cans are considered prohibited objects. There is no bag storage available at the Istana, so ensure your bags don’t have any prohibited items.
Prepare necessary documents: All visitors need to present some form of identification at the main gate, including Singaporeans and Permanent residents. It’s best to bring a form of physical ID (like your IC or your passport).
Bring sunscreen and an umbrella: Sheltered areas at the Istana are few and far between. Given Singapore’s weather, it’s best to prepare for both scorching sun and sudden downpours.
Avoid wheeled sports devices: Bicycles, rollerblades, and personal mobility devices are not allowed on the Istana grounds. However, wheelchairs and prams are allowed and there are dedicated staff onsite to provide assistance.
Be prepared for wet weather: In the event of rainy weather or a lightning risk, the open house may be suspended or cancelled.
Things to do during the Istana Open House
1. Enter the Istana Villa
Photography: The Istana
Built in 1908, the black-and-white bungalow style building previously served as the official residence of the Governor’s Aide-de-Camp, the Private Secretary’s bungalow, and even the Attorney General’s House. It was also used to accommodate state visitors, including the likes of Premier Deng Xiaoping of the People’s Republic of China, Prime Minister Dr. Mahathir Mohamad of Malaysia, and Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau of Canada.
Inside, you’ll find a display of state gifts presented by foreign dignitaries to Singapore’s President and Prime Minister and gallery exhibits with historical mementoes.
Entry into the villa is ticketed and goes to support the President’s Challenge beneficiaries. Only cashless payments like credit or debit cards and QR code payments will be accepted.
Ticketing prices:
Singaporeans & Permanent Residents: $2 per person; children below four years old enter for free
Foreign visitors: Tickets are $10 for adults and $5 for children aged four to 12 years old; children below four years old enter for free
2. Take the Istana Heritage Tour
Photography: The Istana
During the Istana Open House, you can join a one-hour walking tour of the grounds. Quick work considering the Istana spans about 40 hectares of land! Besides the historical buildings, you’ll be treated to sightings of over 250 plant species, and if you’re lucky, you may spot some of the diverse wildlife living in the area.
Tours are conducted in both English and Mandarin, hosted every hour between 9am to 4pm. Be sure to book your slot before going!
Ticketing prices:
Singaporeans & Permanent Residents: $8 per adult; $4 for children aged between four to 12 years old; children under four years old enter for free; family package available
Foreign visitors: $30 per adult, $12 for children
3. Catch live performances and activities
Photography: The Istana
Every open house sees a slew of live performances and family-friendly activities, so there’s always something to see beyond the Istana’s splendour.
…

JB Mount Austin food guide
Yes, cafe hopping in Johor Bahru (JB) is still a thing, and it’ll take more than the long queues at JB customs to deter Singaporeans from exploring good food across the border. For this guide, we’re diving deeper into Mount Austin, a bustling food gem in the city. A 20-minute Grab ride away from JB CIQ, this area is home to many hidden cafes and popular hawker stalls. Read on for our guide to the best JB Mount Austin food spots for your next long weekend getaway!
The current exchange rate is RM1 = ~S$0.31 as of 23 October 2026.
1. Slow Day Cafe
Slow Day Cafe is arguably one of the best matcha cafes in Johor Bahru , serving up hojicha and genmaicha desserts alongside its popular matcha offerings. It’s the perfect pit stop between your shopping spree, where you can sip, eat, and chill with your friends in a warm, cosy space.
We tried two drinks and a dessert: Matcha Strawberry (RM18.90) , Matcha Espresso (RM17.90) , and Genmaicha Nama Cake (RM28) . Between the two drinks, we preferred the Matcha Espresso for its winning combination of earthy matcha flavour and bitter coffee notes. Our favourite, though, was the Genmaicha Nama Cake, starring roasted brown rice, if it sounds appealing to you! In terms of texture, it’s similar to a rich gateau cake that melts in your mouth.
Read our Slow Day Cafe feature .
Address: No. 2-01, Jalan Austin Heights 7/8, Taman Mount Austin, 81100 Johor Bahru, Johor Darul Ta’zim, Malaysia
Opening hours: Mon-Fri 12pm to 6:30pm, Fri-Sun 12pm to 10pm
Website
Slow Day Cafe is not halal-certified.
Slow Day Cafe: Popular Matcha Cafe In JB With Genmaicha Cake And Strawberry Matcha
2. Meow Me Cat House
Many mistake Meow Me Cat House for a pet cafe , where you pay an entrance or cover fee to play with the cats. But that’s not the case, as all you have to do is spend at least RM8 to secure a seat here. This means that you can pet and play with all the adorable cats as long as you get a drink!
There are over 20 kinds of drinks on the menu, ranging from coffee to soda. We tried the signature Tiramisu Latte (RM17) , an iced latte topped with creamy mascarpone, cocoa powder, and ladyfinger biscuits. Their Fizzy Orange Americano (RM17) was equally delicious, featuring a simple concoction of orange juice and Americano, finished with a dried orange atop.
Read our Meow Me Cat House feature.
Address: 28-01, Jalan Austin Height 7/7, Taman Mount Austin, 81100 Johor Bahru, Johor Darul Ta’zim, Malaysia
Opening hours: Thurs-Tue 12pm to 9pm
Website
Meow Me Cat House is not halal-certified.
This JB Cafe Lets You Chill With Cats While Enjoying Tiramisu Latte And Desserts
3. Cheevit Cheeva
Hailing from Bangkok, Cheevit Cheeva is a popular dessert cafe with several branches worldwide—their Malaysian Instagram account alone has more than 9K followers at the time of writing! This trendy cafe specialises in shaved ice desserts that are perfect for a sunny day in JB.
We had to order a shaved ice dessert to see what the hype was all about, so we got the Royal Thai Tea Bingsu (from RM24) to try. This tasty, tea-infused treat boasted a rich, aromatic Thai tea flavour that we thoroughly enjoyed. There were shokupan bits atop the bingsu, which we didn’t find necessary, as the shaved ice was good on its own. If you’re not a fan of bingsu, get the croffle instead. There are five variations to choose from, including Salty Egg Yolk (RM30) and Choco Nutella (RM30) .
Read our Cheevit Cheeva feature .
Address: 23 GF, Jalan Austin Heights 8/1, Taman Mount Austin, 81100 Johor Bahru, Johor Darul Ta’zim, Malaysia
Opening hours: Mon-Thurs 1pm to 11pm, Fri 1pm to 11:30pm, Sat 12:30pm to 11:30pm, Sun 12:30pm to 11pm
Website
Cheevit Cheeva is not halal-certified.
Cheevit Cheeva: Thai-Famous Dessert Cafe In JB With Kunafa Toast And More
4. Jiah Xiang Dim Sum
Dim sum is one of our favourite supper foods for three reasons: it’s affordable, it’s delicious, and many spots open till late. If you’re like us, stop by Jiah Xiang Dim Sum for a late-night meal with your friends.
Our favourite item was the Kataifi Mango Shrimp (RM8.50+) , a sweet-savoury treat that sounded a tad strange at first, but was actually really delicious. You get shrimp and diced mango in a deep-fried crispy pastry that’s made using shredded dough! The Golden Bao (RM8.50+) was also good; an order comes with three buns in a bamboo basket, each filled with a runny salted egg custard that leans sweet and buttery. There are also the must-haves Pork & Chive Dumplings (RM6.80+) and Jiah Xiang Siu Mai (RM6.80+) to substantiate your meal.
Read our Jiah Xiang Dim Sum feature .

Opening hours: Daily 7am to 3pm

Peach Blossoms at PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay has a new à la carte menu from Executive Chinese Chef Edward Chong, launched on 15 October on Level 5 of the hotel.
The menu draws on the Hakka, Teochew, Hokkien, Hainanese and Cantonese traditions that shaped Singapore’s food culture, along with flavours from across South-east Asia. Chef Edward, who is Hakka, put it this way in the release: “As Peach Blossoms embarks on a new chapter, I would like to pay homage to Singapore, a place I have called home for the past 20 years.”
Chicken Rice Tart with 6-Hour Cured Kampachi and Caviar. Photo: PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay
Chicken rice, reworked
The Chicken Rice Tart with 6-Hour Cured Kampachi and Caviar fills a tart shell with rice cooked in chicken fat and aromatics, finished with housemade peanut oil. Kampachi cured for six hours replaces the chicken, a nod to the raw fish dishes of Shunde in Guangdong, and Kaluga Queen caviar adds the saltiness soya sauce would usually bring.
Bak kut teh meets a banquet classic
The Bak Kut Teh Inspired Buddha Jumps Over the Wall simmers pork ribs and chicken with white pepper and spices over a low flame for six hours. That broth holds Jeju abalone, Kanto sea cucumber, South African fish maw and giant king grouper stomach.
Bak Kut Teh Inspired Buddha Jumps Over the Wall. Photo: PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay
Teochew and Hainanese notes
Braised Boston Lobster with basil, Japanese Shiitake mushrooms and preserved radish is cooked in a claypot, the radish being a staple of Teochew kitchens. The Home Styled Braised Marble Goby is dry-braised with a touch of vinegar and served with a separate aromatic curry sauce and pearl rice, a reference to Hainanese scissors-cut curry rice. A squid ink parcel of Spanish mackerel and crab meat takes its spicing from otah.
A refreshed room
In the main dining room, chairs carry mountainscape-inspired upholstery and blown-glass cloud chandeliers hang overhead. Tables have sintered stone tops with built-in lazy Susans, and the Chef’s Table private room is done in embossed burgundy leather.
The refreshed dining room on Level 5. Photo: PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay
The restaurant holds One Diamond in the 2026 Black Pearl Restaurant Guide, sits at No. 78 on the Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants 2026 extended list, and was named among Tatler’s Best 20 Restaurants in Singapore 2026.
Peach Blossoms, Level 5, PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay, 6 Raffles Boulevard. Lunch from 12pm on weekdays and 11.30am on weekends and public holidays, till 3pm; dinner daily 6.30pm to 10.30pm.
Sources: PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay release, 22 October 2026 ; Peach Blossoms .
summary: Peach Blossoms at PARKROYAL COLLECTION Marina Bay has a new à la carte menu from Edward Chong, built on Singapore's dialect cuisines.
title: Peach Blossoms reopens with a Singapore Chinese menu by Edward Chong

This curated guide rounds up some of the best pancake spots across Klang Valley , spotlighting cafes and bakeries that pair thoughtful ingredients with distinctive styles.

1. House of Wheat
House of Wheat wears its popularity subtly, tucked within Mutiara Central yet rarely short of company. From opening hour to late afternoon, the tables tell the story. This is a Cheras favourite that people in Klang Valley return to without fail. The interiors are warm and slightly dim, creating a calm, unhurried mood that suits long brunches and easy conversations.
Sourdough pancakes are the signature here, and for good reason. The Classic Sourdough Pancake (RM13) is simple, gently tangy, and well-balanced, serving as an introduction to the kitchen’s style. Those in the mood for something more indulgent will want to look beyond the basics.
The Chicken Pancake Paradise (RM26) layers sourdough pancakes with crispy fried chicken, finished with amaranth syrup and a sprinkle of nuts, striking a pleasing balance between savoury depth and addicting sweetness.
The Very Berries Pancake (RM23) is a crowd-pleaser, with soft pancakes and cream at the centre, topped with raspberry jam, mixed berries, seeds, and nuts.

2. Common Man Coffee Roasters
Credit – Common Man Coffee Roasters
Common Man Coffee Roasters (CMCR) carries its legacy with stride. A pioneer in coffee roasting, it has long been respected for pairing specialty-grade, ethically sourced coffee with thoughtful food across its Klang Valley outposts. The reputation is built on consistency and craft, and the kitchen mirrors the same discipline found behind the bar.
Credit
Its buttermilk pancakes deserve just as much attention as the coffee. The Common Man Pancakes (RM32) arrive with caramelised bananas, salted caramel sauce, walnut crumble, and berry coulis in a measured balance of richness and freshness.
Credit
For those who lean savoury, the Breakfast Pancakes (RM35) offer a more assertive start to the day. Brown butter pancakes are paired with chilli scrambled eggs, crispy streaky beef, burnt feta, and maple butter syrup, creating layers of flavour that won’t exhaust your taste buds.
Click here to see all outlets’ locations, opening hours, and contact information!
3. Neighbour’s Coffee Bar
Credit
No Klang Valley pancake list feels complete without a souffle entry, and Neighbour’s Coffee Bar fills that role perfectly. Tucked along Seri Gembira Avenue , the cafe offers a cosy, neighbourhood feel that suits slow mornings and lingering brunches. A second outlet at The Hub SS2 in Petaling Jaya extends the appeal, but the mood remains intimate and unfussy.
Credit
Here, the focus is firmly on fuwa fuwa pancakes, airy, delicate, and made to order. The Original Fuwa Fuwa Pancake (RM21) keeps things classic with a freshly baked souffle pancake, nama cream, and housemade syrup. The Berries Fuwa Fuwa Pancake (RM26) adds strawberries and blueberries for a gentle lift of freshness without overpowering the softness beneath.
Click here to see all outlets’ locations, opening hours, and contact information!
4. Yellow Brick Road
Credit
Few brunch names in Klang Valley carry the same instant recognition as Yellow Brick Road at The Five . Long established as a go-to for brunch, desserts, and once-viral tiramisu , it remains a fixture in the city’s dining rhythm. A second outlet in Chinatown widens its reach, but the reputation was cemented well before that expansion.
Credit – Yellow Brick Road
The Minimalist Pancakes (RM17) do exactly what the name suggests, classic pancakes served with maple syrup and butter. Peter Pandan (RM29) pairs pandan pancakes with caramelised and fresh jackfruit, salted caramel ice cream, and gula melaka sauce for a familiar yet elevated flavour profile.
…
summary: Klang Valley’s pancake scene spans sourdough, buttermilk and made-to-order soufflé pancakes, with cafes and bakeries offering both classic stacks and Malaysian-inspired flavours. Prices range from RM13 to RM35, while some venues require reservations for curated sessions, making the roundup useful for brunch diners choosing between casual cafes, dessert-focused spots and more intimate pancake experiences.
title: Best pancake spots in Klang Valley — sourdough, souffle & unique flavours

body:
I bring sad tidings. For those born in the 90s and earlier, you are probably very familiar with Lee Biscuits . You might know their most famous confectionery, the Marie biscuits, simple biscuits perfect with a nice cup of coffee. Their factory at Pontian, Johor , will close by 31 Oct 2026 . While their treats will still be in circulation, we don’t know for certain how long. China Press reported that the factory has no other production plans.
Credit – Google
How about a brief history of the man behind the biscuit? Founder Lee Kong Chian was known as a philanthropist. He spent a large chunk of his fortune funding better education, social welfare and medical research. He ran the brand in Singapore for 21 years before production moved to Malaysia in 1955 . Their biscuits catered to the young and the old. In fact, one of my favourites was the iced gem biscuits. That crunchy, sweet swirl at the top with the buttery biscuit base was oh-so-addictive.
On the other hand, some of my aunts and uncles would have shelves full of Marie biscuits. They would dip them in their, often super sweet, kopi or Milo . Some of their other biscuits include the lemon sandwich biscuits, which have a sweet lemon-flavoured filling. The cream cracker is also a crowd favourite. This might seem gross, but as a kid I microwaved American cheese between 2 cream crackers, which was surprisingly good in a pinch.
Credit – Google
While this is truly sad news, it comes as no surprise. Suppliers and customers were reportedly told in Sep 2026 , and China Press reported that staff are being laid off. Reports from the New Straits Times also mention that the move is part of a restructuring. The group will reportedly focus on core holdings like rubber and palm oil.
Regardless of where they’re headed, Lee Biscuits have cemented their legacy as a brand that gave us affordable, tasty and nostalgic treats. They kept us going throughout the day. I have worked in many a warehouse, and let me tell you, there is at least 1 tin from Lee Biscuits in every one. While they are still on the shelves, I intend to buy some for old times’ sake.
Serangoon Garden Bakery & Confectionary: 41-year-old bakery with nostalgic bakes from $1.20 at Serangoon
summary: Lee Biscuits, the Marie biscuit maker founded in Singapore in 1934, will close its Pontian factory in Johor by the end of Oct 2026. Malaysian media report that suppliers were notified in Sep 2026, staff are being laid off and no future production has been announced, as the parent group refocuses on rubber and palm oil. The news will matter most to those who grew up with its Marie biscuits and iced gem biscuits.
title: Lee Biscuits – 92-year-old Marie biscuit maker to end production by end of Oct 2026
