Not all of us have a sweet tooth. I personally prefer the succulent and savoury bites of a good steak. But I will say Hues Caneles is very close to turning me to the dark side. Located near a hawker centre in Chinatown , they serve beautiful French pastries and bakes you’d find in the streets of Paris.
I can’t talk about Hues Caneles without talking about the interior itself. When you enter this quaint bakery, the first thing you feel is warmth. Warmth from the orange light painting the room. Autumn vibes from the aroma of spices and baked goods that pours into the main room from the kitchen in the back. The decor is industrial with some whimsical accoutrements placed about.
Even the placement of the menu, the chalkboard and the adorable drawings of the caneles add levity to the place. Traditionally, a canele has rum in it. According to the owner, Ku Nurizwanshah, rum is important to ensure the outside of the pastry caramelises properly, due to its sugar content. He mentions that he has a secret ingredient to replicate this effect.
Unfortunately, I was unable to get it out of him. I’ll be sure to try again on my next visit.
What to order at Hues Caneles
I won’t beat around the bush. Their caneles overall are an absolute delight. I got the Taro (S$5.50) , Creme brulee (S$5.50) and Salted caramel (S$5.50) . I would suggest following this sequence of flavours should you try all three. Each flavour gets more and more intense, so it might affect lighter flavours should you try it out of the order I mentioned.
The taro ’s texture was unexpected. I figured it would be smooth and creamy, but it actually had a pleasant bite to it. I could feel my teeth sink into the filling. The taro flavour itself is not overpowering. There is no artificial taste, just a light, sweet potato-ey accent you experience at the very end.
That and the canele itself are complementary to each other. The shell of the canele is like glass, in the best way possible. The moment you break it, you are treated to a soft, spongy centre. You can taste the different spices. It’s warm and fragrant, making the pastry feel not too rich.
19 best places in Telok Ayer for foodies to discover
The creme brulee was smooth and creamy. The custard taste was not overpowering; the eggy flavour lends itself to the caramelised shell of the canele . The glassy top wasn’t really present, but that’s completely fine, since the entire canele felt like a crisp layer of sugar glass.
And last but definitely not least, the salted caramel . This is easily my favourite flavour, but I will say it might not be for everyone. It has that almost sickly sweet butterscotch flavour. What sets this apart from the others is the bitterness. It is almost savoury and contrasts with the sweetness nicely.
Who is Hues Caneles best for?
If you are looking to try something new, try Hues Caneles. The canele is a unique pastry that is a rare find in Singapore. The fact that it is Muslim-owned makes it even more rare. The taste of each pastry is delicious but, most importantly, balanced – something you can enjoy without feeling sick. There is also coffee, sandwiches and much more.
Also, I think their caneles , along with their other treats, make the perfect gift. They are small, pretty, and their packaging is also very eye-catching and pleasant.
How to get to Hues Caneles
The nearest MRT is Maxwell, which is a 5-minute walk to Hues Caneles. The nearest bus stop is New Bridge Centre , which is only 2 minutes away. Hues Caneles is at 4 Sago Lane, #02-123, Kreta Ayer Heights, Singapore 050004. Look for the stairs near the drop-off point, and you should spot their cute logo from the bottom floor.
Do we recommend Hues Caneles?
Yes, easily. They have some of the best-tasting Muslim-owned bakes I’ve had in a while. Do note that they are constantly updating their menu, so the caneles I’ve tried here might not be around when you visit. Their menu rotates seasonally so they stay fresh and creative.
I also ordered extra pastries for my family and noticed how gently and carefully the owner packed them. Their paper bag even included reheating instructions. They arrived in pristine condition, and that attention to detail deserves praise.
People also read:
Where to find the best Croissants in Singapore?
Where to find the best Bakeries in Singapore?
summary: Hues Caneles is a Muslim-owned bakery on Sago Lane in Chinatown, serving caneles in taro, creme brulee and salted caramel flavours at S$5.50 each. The pastries have a glass-like shell and a soft, spiced centre that stays balanced rather than overly rich, with the salted caramel adding a bitter, almost savoury contrast. It suits first-time canele eaters and anyone after small, giftable bakes, and is a 5-minute walk from Maxwell MRT.
title: Hues Caneles: How an ex-engineer turned Muslim-owned canelé-making Into a science

BAO Fast Foods (BFF) is a new concept from London’s cult-favourite BAO . After a homecoming run in Taiwan, the pop-up will next land in Singapore at New Bahru from 11 November 2026 to 28 December 2026 .
But what exactly is this experience that is part fast food joint , part Asian convenience store ? Keep reading to find out more!
Credit: BAO
For those of you who enjoy exploring convenience stores when you’re overseas, especially in Asian countries like Taiwan, you will find the vibes here immaculate. At BFF, there will be a sense of familiarity with a distinct Taiwan flavour.
Credit: BAO
Expect shelves filled with Taiwanese comfort food and snacks , and a rotating selection of grab-and-go items. There will also be self-serve stations and sections featuring BAO’s merchandise .
From protein-packed bites like Egg Sandos and Marinated Eggs to high-fibre sides like “Fried Rice” Quinoa and Golden Kimchi , to sweet treats like Soy Puddings with tiramisu and banoffee toppings, you’ll have plenty to discover and revisit the pop-up for.
Credit: BAO
The signature item, however, is the Chicken Chopper (S$6.50) . Of course, when it comes to Taiwanese snacks, you must have fried chicken . And this is BFF’s take on the classic street food, perfected over 140 iterations.
You will notice that the chicken is cut with the bone left in place as a handle, making it easy to eat. By dipping the chicken in a soymilk batter and coating it in a tapioca starch mix, BFF ensures the meat stays juicy while having a light, crackly crust on the outside.
Flavours to look forward to include Original Crispy , Flame Glazed , and Master Scalded . The first is seasoned with Taiwanese white pepper, the second is flavoured with soy-garlic or mala hot honey glaze, and the third is dipped in a boiling soy-based master sauce with star anise and cinnamon.
Credit: BAO
For a more filling meal, you can order the Chicken Chopper as part of a rice box (S$7.95) , or pair it with Dan Dan Noodles (S$6.50) or Beef Cup Noodle (S$12.50) . Combos from S$9.50 are also available.
Credit: BAO
Another staple of Taiwanese food culture is tea ! And you will be able to find a selection of Taiwanese craft tea here at the BFF pop-up. Highlights include the nitro-infused Fluffy Natural Alishan Wintermelon (S$5.95) , the carbonated Orange Guava Beauty Tea (S$6.50) , and the rich Original Peanut Oatside Milk (S$6) .
If anything about this pop-up excites you, mark your calendars from 11 November to 28 December. It’s time to have a date at the convenience store!

11 November 2026 to 28 December 2026

Tampines 1 Level 3 revamp
Much like those up in the North-East, Easties are absolutely blessed when it comes to the amount of shopping haunts they can hit up. You’d be hard-pressed not to find a mall within walking distance here – and then we have the multiple in Tampines alone.
The 3 malls have been a stalwart inclusion throughout my 27 years living in the East, ever-changing and growing beside me. Tampines 1’s Level 3 has received a major revamp, and you’ll now be able to shop at your usual faves as well as spot several new inclusions to the mall’s directory. Here’s what you can expect when you swing by for a visit in the near future.
1. Box Hunt
Huge range of blind boxes & other hobby-related finds like TCG
Image for illustration purposes only.
We all know how rabid Singaporeans can get whenever cute ling ling long longs are involved; thankfully, you’ll be able to get your fair share of bits and bobs at Box Hunt . Here, blind boxes stretch to as far as the eye can see, so you can bet good money that you’ll find one from your favourite IP.
Image credit: Box Hunt SG via Facebook
If the stock at their other outlets are anything to go by, you’ll be able to snag blind boxes from franchises such as Butterbear, Winnie the Pooh, Sanrio, and Smiski to name a few. There’ll be tables in-store dedicated to trading and game sessions, making Box Hunt a go-to hangout spot for TCG fans. Plus, their Facebook page prominently features products from both the One Piece and Pokémon trading card games.
From what we’ve heard, Box Hunt’s Tampines 1 outlet is celebrating their reopening with a Buy 3 Get 1 Free promotion on their blind boxes, so if you’d like to add some heft to your collection, you know where to head. If you’re into console gaming as well, don’t miss out on the shop’s selection of Nintendo Switch titles.
Unit number: #03-19
Opening date: End-October 2026
Contact: Box Hunt Instagram
2. Geláre
Popular dessert spot with ice cream waffles, croffles & milkshakes
For a sweet treat, look no further than Geláre . The dessert parlour needs no introduction; with 5 other locations across the country, it’s clear that their yummy confections have won the hearts and taste buds of many.
Image credit: Geláre
They’re known for their freshly-baked waffles (from $9.90) which are satisfyingly crisp on the outside, while still being light and fluffy on the inside. What’s more, each waffle comes with a sinful dollop of rich, creamy ice cream that’s made with less than 5% air for a denser texture and a punch of flavour that’s nothing short of addictive.
Image credit: Geláre
Also on the menu are a slew of croffles (from $6.90) , sundaes (from $9.10) , and milkshakes (from $7.90) to reward yourself with after an honest day of work.
To mark new beginnings, Geláre’s Tampines 1 outlet will be bringing diners 4 weeks of 1-for-1 specials when they open. Bring a buddy and head down to double up on treats such as waffles, single-scoop ice creams, coffee and mocktails, and croffles.
Unit number: #03-K6
Opening date: End-October 2026
Contact: Geláre website
3. KPOP HOUSE
K-Pop haven with the latest albums & regular fan events
Image for illustration purposes only.
Image credit: SingMalls
K-Pop fans, you’re in luck. Tampines 1 now has a one-stop shop for all your K-Pop needs in KPOP HOUSE . It’s one of the mall’s newest openings, and will begin welcoming visitors at the end of October, but don’t let that stop you from putting together your wishlist.
Plenty of time to get your light sticks ready for when LE SSERAFIM & BABYMONSTER pay Singapore a visit later this year.
Image credit: Source Music
Expect the store to stock the latest albums from the hottest K-Pop artists, from chart-topping heavy hitters like CORTIS, LE SSERAFIM, ILLIT, and ATEEZ. You’ll be able to shop for merch from your favorite groups too, such as light sticks, trinkets, and apparel to make sure your get-up is completely concert-ready. The store will also have a dedicated space for fan-held events, so keep an eye out for upcoming celebrations of your fave idol groups.
Image credit: Tampines 1
BTW , we’ve received word that KPOP HOUSE will be having a storewide discount of 8% , a promotion which runs from when they open till 31st December 2026 . While you’re there, check out STiiKERS, a sticker customisation experience straight from Korea. KPOP HOUSE is one of the first few establishments in Singapore to offer this service.
It allows you to customise photo stickers with various K-Pop idol group logos and other cute graphics, and the printed sticker sheet creates mini versions of yourself so you can stick it on photo cards as if you’re posing with your idol bias!

Claw machine & gachapon galore
…

Upcoming card shows & conventions in Singapore
Whether you’re a seasoned Magic: The Gathering player or just started out collecting Pokémon cards , card shows and conventions are one of the best ways to hunt for rare finds, pick up new additions for your binder, and bond with fellow Trading Card Game (TCG) enthusiasts.
Thankfully, there are plenty of opportunities for you to dive deeper into the hobby, from small weekend trade shows to large-scale conventions. Here are some of the upcoming card shows in Singapore to keep on your radar for your next TCG spending spree.
What are card shows & conventions?
Image credit: @sgcardshow via Instagram
If you’re new to the trading card scene, card shows are events where TCG fans gather to buy , sell , and trade cards , browse pop-culture collectables , or even take part in TCG tournaments to win prizes.
Popular TCGs include Pokémon, Riftbound, and One Piece, and you’ll find vendors selling everything from booster packs and sealed products to graded cards sealed in protective cases, also known as slabs.
Beyond being a marketplace, these events are also a chance for fans to meet fellow TCG players, build connections with dealers face-to-face, and share their passion for the hobby. Most card conventions take place over the weekends, with many offering free entry, though some shows may require registration or have paid tickets with additional perks.
1. Asia Cards & Collectible Expo
6 weekends from 24th October to 13th December 2026
View this post on Instagram
Arcade chain Cow Play Cow Moo (CPCM) is bringing back the Asia Cards & Collectible Expo , taking place over 6 weekends. Held at the atrium outside its Suntec City outlet, CPCM promises an even more exciting experience for collectors, with plenty of opportunities to search for the chase card you’re looking for.
For the 1st weekend, visitors can look forward to the Moo-Bladers Club , a community-driven Beyblade X tournament. Entry into the tournament costs $22 , with participants receiving $20 worth of CPCM tokens and a complimentary drink . Even if you’re not there to shop for cards, you can still join in the fun and let it rip with Beyblade fans.
While details for the other activities haven’t been confirmed yet, previous editions featured drawing contests, lucky draws, and dedicated playing zones where you can learn how to play TCGs like Pokémon and Magic: The Gathering.
Admission: Free
Date: 24th-25th Oct, 31st Oct-1st Nov, 7th-8th Nov, 28th-29 Nov, 5th-6th Dec & 12th-13th Dec 2026
Time: 10am-10pm
Address: Level 3, Suntec City Tower 3 & 4 Atrium, 3 Temasek Blvd, Singapore 038983
2. SG Collectibles & Card Show
Happening on weekends from October to December 2026
Image credit: SG Collectibles & Card Show
SG Collectibles & Card Show (SCCS) is a community-driven convention designed to bring collectors and gaming enthusiasts together in an offline space, with 3 editions coming up in the next 3 months, each with its own unique theme.
Get into the spooky spirit with the Halloween edition taking place in October, or kick off your year-end shopping early at the shopping season edition in November, which falls on the weekend between Black Friday and Cyber Monday. The final edition held in December will be Christmas-themed, rounding off the year with festive cheers and TCG fun.
Beyond collecting, SCCS also frequently partners with community groups to support good causes through games and activities. Join charity auctions featuring original artworks by local artists, or take part in trade-down challenges , where you exchange items that progressively go down in value throughout the event, with all proceeds going to charity.
Admission: Free
Date: 24th-25th Oct, 28th-29th Nov & 19th-20th Dec 2026
Time: 11am-9pm
Address: #03-02, Perennial Business City, 1 Venture Avenue, Singapore 608521
3. NEXUS TCG Tradeshow
4 weekends from 24th October 2026 to 24th January 2027
Image adapted from: @thenexustradeshow via Instagram
If you’re looking to add to your collection or score your next big hit, check out the NEXUS TCG Tradeshow . The October 2026 edition will feature over 50 vendors selling sealed products, graded slabs, and TCG accessories spanning Pokémon, sports, and more.
With 6 dates remaining in 2026, you can drop by the convention at The Centrepoint for free from 11am to 9pm . If you’re looking to start 2027 by expanding your card collection, the NEXUS TCG Tradeshow will be at the Suntec Convention Centre on 23rd and 24th January 2027 , with more details for these shows to be announced.
Admission: Free
Date: 24th-25th Oct 2026, 14th-15th Nov 2026, 19th-20th Dec 2026 & 23rd-24th Jan 2027
Time: 11am-9pm | 11am-8am (23rd & 24th Jan 2027)
Address: #03-07 The Centrepoint, 176 Orchard Road, Singapore 238843 | Suntec Convention Centre Hall 405, 1 Raffles Boulevard, Singapore 039593 (23rd & 24th Jan 2027)
4. Award X Halloween Trade Night
1 day only on 30th October 2026
Image credit: @cj_collectiblez via Instagram

Aesthetic ZUS Coffee outlets in Malaysia
Sometimes, a good cup of coffee is best enjoyed with a view. Even if the coffee isn’t life-changing, a pretty setting can make all the difference. While cafes in Singapore with scenic views are hard to come by, with many tucked inside malls or surrounded by high-rise buildings, Malaysian coffee chain ZUS Coffee has outlets blessed with views worth slowing down for.
If you frequently visit our neighbours across the Causeway, we’ve rounded up some of the most scenic ZUS Coffee outlets worth checking out. All of them are in popular spots, making them easy to add to your next trip to Malaysia.
1. ZUS Coffee – MAHA Tower Langkawi
Located under one of Langkawi’s most iconic landmarks
Image adapted from: @zus.coffee via Instagram
No, you’re not looking at a mini Eiffel Tower, but rather Langkawi’s MAHA Tower , which is also home to one of the island’s coolest ZUS Coffee outlets. Tucked at the base of the 138m-tall tower, the outlet sits beneath Langkawi’s tallest landmark, whose architecture blends futuristic steel and glass with geometric designs inspired by local folklore.
Image credit: Amira Nadja Mohamed Nasran via Google Maps
Not keen on sitting in the air-conditioned outlet? Head to the outdoor seating area for unobstructed views of the surrounding Andaman Sea.
Alternatively, pay a little extra to take your drink up to the tower’s sky decks, where you’ll be treated to breathtaking 360° panoramic views. Don’t forget to snap some photos while you are there!

If you’re craving a little countryside escape without driving too far from JB Sentral, ZUS Coffee at Setia Eco Garden in Gelang Patah might just be the spot for you. One of the more unique entries on our list is ZUS Coffee Meets Pastry at Selangor’s 1 Utama Shopping Centre , which offers more than the usual coffee. Located near 1 Utama’s indoor FlowRider and skate park, the outlet is a fun pit stop to grab a bite while taking a breather from shopping. If you’re craving ZUS Coffee’s usual drinks instead, there’s also a regular ZUS Coffee outlet at Level 2 in the mall.

Best Japanese food brand openings in Singapore in 2026
Our little red dot is home to a variety of cuisines from all over the world, yet in the midst of it all, Japanese food seems to steal our hearts time and time again. With Japan being one of Singaporeans’ go-to travel destinations, it’s no surprise that there’s been a recent wave of Japanese brands making their debut here. From famous gyudon to matcha desserts and Ginza-famous sandos, here’s our compilation of the best new Japanese eateries in 2026 .
1. Matsuya
Image credit: u/kccz123 via Reddit
If you’re a frequent Japan-goer, you’d know that Matsuya is one of Japan’s most popular gyudon chains. Now, you can save your flight to Japan, as they’re set to make their arrival at Suntec City sometime in November 2026 . This would mark the completion of the ‘big 3’ gyudon chains in SG, alongside Sukiya and Yoshinoya.
Image credit: Japan Journeys
While we still don’t know much about the Singapore outlet, Matsuya is well-loved and known for its affordable gyudon bowls. A full meal in Japan costs roughly between ¥400 and ¥1000 , which converts to about S$3.25 to S$8.10 . The top pick here is the classic Beef Bowl (¥480) that’s stewed with onions in a sweet soy sauce. For a heartier option, go for their selection of curry bowls, such as Beef Curry and Rice (¥680) or Beef Curry with Cheese (¥950) .
Read our Matsuya feature .
Address: 3 Temasek Boulevard, #B1-125 (Tower 2), Singapore 038983
Opening hours: TBD
Website
Matsuya is not halal-certified.
Popular Japanese Gyudon Chain To Open At Suntec In Nov 2026
2. I’m Donut
Image credit: The New Yorker
Adding to the line-up of Japanese doughnut chains, I’m Donut will be making its debut in Singapore at ION Orchard , set to open in December 2026 . The brand has over 10 outlets across Japan and is best known for their fluffy nama doughnuts. What sets them apart is their brioche dough, made with pumpkin and fermented at low temperatures before it gets fried at high heat.
Image credit: I’m Donut
Though their Singapore menu is still unconfirmed, we presume that their best-selling powdered sugar doughnut, the I’m Donut? Original (price TBD) , will make an appearance. Another top pick would be the Custard Cream (price TBD) , filled generously with Diplomat cream. The I’m Donut? Matcha (price TBD) would be perfect for fellow matcha fans, starring a kneaded dough coated in Yame matcha powder from Fukuoka. FYI: everything here is made handmade in-house, from the dough to the fillings and even the toppings!
Check out our I’m Donut coverage .
Address: 2 Orchard Turn, #B2-19, ION Orchard, Singapore 238801
Opening hours: TBD
Website
I’m Donut is not halal-certified.
Viral Japanese Chain I’m Donut To Open At ION Orchard
3. Age.3
Image credit: @age.3_ginza
Another Japanese eatery landing at ION Orchard in mid-November 2026 is Age.3 , a fried sando shop hailing all the way from Ginza. The brand rose to fame for its crispy golden sando boasting a soft and chewy centre, with locals braving the queues of up to two hours just to try them.
Image credit: @age.3_ginza
Going all-out for their debut, the Singapore menu will feature a whopping 34 flavours. For something sweet and classic, opt for the Whipped Cream Sando (price TBD) that’s made with low-sugar cream that’s whipped by hand. Other interesting flavours include the Creme Brulee Sando (price TBD) , Mont Blanc (price TBD) , and Chocolate Strawberry (price TBD) . Their savoury choices are just as extensive, including the Beef Short Rib Yakiniku Sando (price TBD) served with barbecue sauce and a soft-cooked egg, Grilled Keema Curry (price TBD) , and Grilled Cheese with Smoked Salmon (price TBD) .
Read our Age.3 feature .
Address: ION Orchard, Singapore 238801
Opening hours: TBD
Website
Age.3 is not halal-certified.
Viral Japanese Fried Sando Shop Age.3 To Open At ION Orchard With 34 Flavours
4. O/sio
Image credit: O/sio
Following our review of Sio Pasta —an Italian-inspired pasta concept helmed by Michelin-approved Japanese chef Shusaku Toba—earlier this year, its sister eatery, O/Sio , is set to launch its first overseas eatery in Tanjong Pagar on 4 November 2026 . O/Sio offers hearty Italian fare with a Japanese twist, from fresh pasta to charcoal-grilled meats, alongside a complementary wine programme curated by Chef Toba himself.
Image credit: O/sio
Look forward to mains starting from $18.80 . Special offerings include the Singapore-exclusive Smoked Truffle Carbonara (price TBD) for a decadent pairing of creamy pasta and earthy black truffle shavings. If you enjoy seafood, the Seafood Pomodoro (price TBD) would be right up your alley. They also have the fan-favourite Charcoal-grilled Angus Beef Steak (price TBD) that’s served with a side of crispy fries.
Read our O/sio feature .
Address: 38 Tanjong Pagar Road, Singapore 088461
Opening hours: TBD
Tel: 8072 9512
Website
O/Sio is not halal-certified.

A festival for photographers is happening in Singapore right now, and another one is also on the horizon! But this time, the festival is for the writers.
The annual Singapore Writers Festival (SWF) 2026 returns from 13 to 22 November 2026 , featuring literary experiences for all you bookworms, mystery lovers , and anyone looking for things to do in November.
If you’re wondering what activities are worth exploring across the different festival venues, we’ve got you covered.
Hidden in Plain Sight
Credit: Singapore Writers Festival 2026
The theme of this year’s SWF is ‘Hidden in Plain Sight’. The festival invites readers , writers, and visitors to look beyond the surface and uncover stories they might otherwise miss. This is especially apparent with the crime-and-mystery-themed programmes at SWF 2026.
Credit: Singapore Writers Festival 2026
One highlight is The Making of a Serial Killer , a panel featuring authors of psychological thriller , mystery , and crime genres. Some of you might recognise one of them, Seo Mi-ae , a South Korean writer known for her award-winning mystery thrillers.
This panel, taking place on 14 November 2026 at Victoria Theatre , will explore the authors’ creative process in creating characters and crafting stories.
Credit: Singapore Writers Festival 2026
If you’d like something more interactive, try an interactive mystery activity on the SWF website – The Verdict is Yours . You will investigate The Case of the Vanishing Diamond , which leads to 10 different conclusions , each submitted by a young writer.
Vote for your favourite and stand a chance to win a 2-day, 1-night stay at The Fullerton Hotel .
Live Storytelling
Credit: Orang Laut SG
Want to experience storytelling with lived experience? Islands of Memories: Stories from the Southern Sea will take you on a coastal walk on 14 November 2026 and 21 November 2026 .
You will hear stories about the Orang Laut and Orang Pulau communities , enjoy a shared meal , and discover histories and stories along the way. This event is ticketed at S$80 and is SG Culture Pass eligible . Find out more and purchase your tickets here .
Credit: Kotuwa
If you like the idea of gathering around a table for a meal while hearing stories, this one’s for you. The Salon with Jemimah Wei will let you hear from the Singaporean author as she explores topics such as daughterhood and family expectations.
This conversation, based on Jemimah’s debut novel, The Original Daughter , will be held on 19 November 2026 at Kotuwa at New Bahru . Canapes and drinks will be served. Tickets are S$60 and are available to book with SG Culture Pass here .
Festival Passes
Credit: Singapore Writers Festival 2026
If you want to explore a wide range of programmes at SWF 2026, consider purchasing a Festival Pass , which costs S$30 for adults and just S$15 for youths . This pass will give you access to more than 100 selected programmes . Check out what is included here , as some sessions require separate tickets.
Festival Passes can also be purchased using your SG Culture Pass credits , so if you have any left to spare, you know what to do! To explore all programmes at SWF 2026, including both free and ticketed events, visit SWF’s website .

body:
Barossa Steak & Grill has reopened on the VivoCity waterfront as Barossa 2.0. The Australian steakhouse and bar, run by homegrown group Creative Eateries, came back on 17 October with a new à la carte menu by chef Dylan Ong, and the Josper charcoal oven sits at the centre of it.
Steak on the grill at Barossa. Image: Barossa Steak & Grill
The menu, section by section
The new menu runs from bread and oysters through to boards for the table, with chef’s signatures marked on every page. Prices are before service charge and GST.
• Bread and butter: S$4 to S$15
• Starters: S$7 to S$32
• Soups: S$5 to S$22
• Hot plates: S$14 to S$32
• Mains and pasta: S$26 to S$42
• From the Josper: S$20 to S$88
• For the table: S$89 to S$189
• Desserts: S$18 to S$29
The bread comes with a choice of two house butters, kombu butter with kelp, nori and sea salt, or lemon whipped brown butter with soy sauce. Both are sold in 180g jars at S$15 to take home. Australian market oysters with a chardonnay mignonette are S$7 each.
The Barossa 2.0 menu at a glance. Screenshot: barossa.com.sg
From the Josper
Every steak from the charcoal oven comes with confit garlic, seasonal pickles and one sauce, from red wine beef jus and green peppercorn to tarragon béarnaise, chimichurri and black truffle mustard. The kitchen recommends medium-rare for beef and lamb. Among the chef’s signature cuts:
• Australian Wagyu 6-7 MB striploin: S$36 per 100g
• Australian Pure Black Angus coulotte MB 4-5: S$44
• 1.2kg Australian Black Angus tomahawk for sharing: S$189
Grilled king tiger prawns, one of the 2.0 menu’s chef’s signatures. Image: Barossa Steak & Grill
Beyond steak
Non-beef eaters have a real choice. Signatures include grilled king tiger prawns with prawn head butter (S$28), wild-caught charred octopus with nduja (S$32), and a whole Josper-grilled lemon sole with mussel cream (S$42). The 36-hour Shiraz-braised beef cheek is S$32, and lobster bisque is S$22. Desserts include a sticky date pudding with burnt butter ice cream (S$19) and a Bombe Alaska flambéed (S$29).
Families get a kids menu from S$15 to S$18. The restaurant is not halal-certified, and several dishes contain pork.
Barossa Steak & Grill is at 1 HarbourFront Walk, #01-161/162, VivoCity. Reservations are taken online and through its concierge line on +65 8303 1863.
summary: Barossa Steak & Grill reopened at VivoCity on 17 October as Barossa 2.0, with a new à la carte menu by chef Dylan Ong centred on its Josper charcoal oven, from S$7 oysters to a S$189 tomahawk.
title: Barossa Steak & Grill reopens at VivoCity with a Josper-led 2.0 menu by Dylan Ong

body:
Shake Shack’s white truffle menu is back at its Singapore shacks, and this year the beef and mushroom burgers have company. The burger chain has added a white truffle chicken burger to the line-up, which runs while stocks last.
Shake Shack’s white truffle menu is back for autumn. Image: Shake Shack Singapore
What is on the white truffle menu
Every item uses a white truffle sauce made with real white truffle, and all the burgers come on a toasted potato bun.
• White Truffle Burger: a quarter-pound Angus beef patty with emmental, white truffle sauce and crispy onions, as a single or double
• White Truffle ‘Shroom: a crisp-fried portobello filled with Monterey Jack, Tilsiter and Colby cheeses, over shredded lettuce
• White Truffle Chicken: hand-breaded crispy chicken breast or thigh over the truffle sauce and arugula, with pickled shallot
• White Truffle Fries: crinkle-cut fries dusted with grated parmesan, with the truffle sauce on the side
HungryGoWhere puts the beef burger at S$14.20 for a single patty, the chicken burger at S$12.20 and the fries at S$8.90.
The new White Truffle Chicken. Image: Shake Shack Singapore
A new season, and a new burger
The menu first reached Singapore in April 2024, a year after Shake Shack launched white truffle in the US, HungryGoWhere reports. Earlier runs came in spring. This one moves to October, in step with the Italian white truffle season, and the chicken burger is the first new item since the original trio.
The White Truffle Table on 7 November
Shake Shack is also hosting a one-night tasting, The White Truffle Table, at its VivoCity shack on 7 November from 6.30pm. The evening adds freshly shaved white truffle at the table and complimentary wine. HungryGoWhere reports that tickets had sold out by the time it published.
White Truffle Fries, served with the truffle sauce on the side. Image: Shake Shack Singapore
Holiday custard alongside
The truffle line-up shares the counter with Shake Shack’s holiday series. This year’s festive frozen custard flavour is mint chocolate fudge, served in the Minter Wonderland cup with whipped cream, chocolate pearls, feuilletine, fudge sauce and a gingerbread man cookie, from S$8.40 for a single. There is also a hazelnut chocolate crunch shake at S$10.60, built on vanilla frozen custard with salted chocolate hazelnut paste and toasted hazelnuts.
summary: Shake Shack's white truffle menu is back in Singapore while stocks last, with the beef burger, 'Shroom burger and fries joined by a new white truffle chicken burger, plus a mint chocolate fudge holiday custard.
title: Shake Shack brings back white truffle burgers, now with a chicken version

Ahoy, anime fans and Bikini Bottom residents ! Two beloved fictional worlds are colliding as McDonald’s Malaysia introduces its latest Happy Meal collection , featuring SpongeBob SquarePants characters reimagined as members of the Straw Hat Pirates .
Credit – McDonald’s
Recently launched on 22 Oct 2026 , the limited-edition SpongeBob x One Piece Happy Meal toys feature 10 collectibles released in pairs over 5 weeks .
From SpongeBob as Luffy to Patrick as Zoro, the crossover brings together familiar faces in unexpected ways, making this collection worth checking out for fans of both franchises.
Credit – McDonald’s Malaysia
The first two toys, SpongeBob x Luffy and Patrick x Zoro , arrive on 22 Oct , followed by Squidward x Sanji and Sandy x Nami on 29 Oct . On 5 Nov , look out for Mr. Krabs x Jinbe and Gary x Chopper , before Larry x Franky and Plankton x Usopp join the collection on 12 Nov .
The final pair, Smitty Werbenjäger­manjensen x Brook and Pearl x Robin , rounds things off on 19 Nov .
With 10 characters to collect, you might find yourself making a few extra McDonald’s runs over the coming weeks. They could also make cute additions to your desk or One Piece merchandise collection, especially if you have a soft spot for these underwater misfits.
Credit – McDonald’s Malaysia
Getting your hands on the toys is easy, too. Each McDonald’s Malaysia Happy Meal comes with a free toy , while stocks last. You can grab yours through McDelivery , at the Drive-Thru or by visiting your nearest McDonald’s restaurant .
There are several meals to choose from, including Chicken Burger , 4-piece Chicken McNuggets , Cheeseburger , Ayam Goreng McD , Sausage McMuffin and 2-piece Hotcakes .
Ready to set sail for the Grand Line with your favourite Bikini Bottom characters? Keep an eye on the release schedule and grab your Happy Meal before your favourite toys disappear. The hunt for all 10 collectibles starts now!

body:
Char kway teow is a hawker dish that’s not very well received as it has a reputation of being oily and sinful, but it’s also one of my top 3 local food picks that I indulge in every now and then. 409 AMK Market And Food Centre reopened on 8 Aug 2026 and for this round’s friendly battle, I decided to pit 2 stalls from there — Bendemeer Fresh Cockles Fried Kway Teow and Har Mee , a relatively new addition to the hawker centre.
What is char kway teow ?
With its strong roots in the Teochew community, char kway teow is a dish I grew up eating, all thanks to my late paternal Teochew grandmother, who used to sell it alongside carrot cake at an army canteen. It’s a noodle dish that combines flat kway teow and yellow mee , stir-fried to wok hei gloriousness together with dark/light soy sauce, sambal , oyster sauce, kecap manis , tau geh , fishcake, lup cheong , cockles, pork lard, and egg.
What makes a good char kway teow ?
Everyone has differing opinions on what makes a great plate of char kway teow . Personally, I feel it should have a good balance of sweet and savoury, possess a decent amount of wok hei , and be perfumed with the taste and aroma of pork lard.
Why these contenders?
In 2025, Bendemeer Fresh Cockles Fried Kway Teow made headlines when the owner passed on his char kway teow cooking skills to his special needs son. After being diagnosed with cancer and with his wife having suffered a stroke, he had considered folding the business for good. However, the encouragement of his regular customers gave him the strength to keep the stall going. On the other hand, Har Mee is a newer addition that relocated from a nearby neighbourhood kopitiam . Run by a Singaporean man and his Thai wife, the stall specialises in prawn noodles but also serves char kway teow , which the wife is in charge of frying.
Bendemeer Fresh Cockles Fried Kway Teow
I watched as the son took his time to fry the char kway teow orders plate by plate, with his mum closely supervising him. The stall offers S$4.50 and S$5.50 portions. As the plates of char kway teow were distributed to the customers before me, they left behind a fragrant smoky aroma in its wake.
After the first mouthful of my S$4.50 plate, I felt that the char kway teow had a classic, old-school nostalgic flavour with decent wok hei that is relatively difficult to find. Mind you, this was not cooked by an experienced uncle but by a much younger person who recently learnt the ropes. Needless to say, I was impressed.
The flavour of the sweet sauce was on the stronger side and as for someone who loves his char kway teow on the sweet side, this was got me excited! The noodles were on the wetter side, with a mild peppery kick that crept in towards the end of each mouthful.
The rest of the ingredients were awesome — the lup cheong was flavourful, cockles were fresh and plump, and the fishcake was great. If I had one tiny complaint, it would be the lack of pork lard. I only got to enjoy one or two small pieces and I wished there was more to enhance the overall unctuousness.
Har Mee
Har Mee offers Char Kway Teow in 3 different sizes — S$4.50 , S$5.50 , and S$6.50 . When my S$4.50 plate arrived, my eyes lit up at the generous portion; it was slightly larger than the one served at the other stall.The noodles also looked noticeably drier and lighter. True to its appearance, the kway teow mee was less sweet than its competitor’s. I reckon those who prefer Penang-style char kway teow would take to this version better.
The wok flavour was present, though it didn’t quite pack the same punch as the one from Bendemeer. Flavour-wise, the noodles were savoury and delicious, with a mild peppery kick that crept in towards the end of each bite. What made me even happier was discovering 5 to 6 pieces of pork lard scattered throughout the plate — a shiok bonus, indeed!
Verdict
Bendemeer Fresh Cockles Fried Kway Teow
Har Mee
Price
S$4.50/S$5.50
S$4.50/S$5.50/S$6.50
Portion
Can be slightly more generous
Decent amount
Flavour
Great with sufficient wok hei, a little on the sweeter side
Great with more subtle wok hei , leaning towards savoury
Ingredient Quality
No complaints
Rather than me revealing who the winner is right now, let me pose the question back to you — what’s your favourite rendition of char kway teow ? If you’re like me who prefers a wetter style with sufficient wok flavour and sweet notes, then Bendemeer Fresh Cockles Fried Kway Teow is the place for you. Otherwise, if a slightly more savoury version with slightly lesser wok hei interests you more, then I’ll recommend Har Mee.
This char kway teow showdown was a tough one, as both stalls were almost neck and neck. Ultimately, it came down to my personal preferences, and after much deliberation, I hereby crown Bendemeer Fresh Cockles Fried Kway Teow the winner of this round!

summary: 409 AMK Market and Food Centre, which reopened on 8 August 2026, is home to two contrasting char kway teow stalls: Bendemeer Fresh Cockles Fried Kway Teow and Har Mee. Both offer plates from S$4.50, with differences in sweetness, wok hei, texture and pork lard. This comparison helps diners choose between a sweeter, wetter rendition and a drier, more savoury version, with Bendemeer emerging as the overall winner.

body:
Craving a little spice before your flight? How about a lot of spice? Well, Mala Mia , which opened on 14 Aug 2026 at Changi Airport T3 , is the place to get your fix. And to all my Muslim friends, it’s officially halal-certified as of 12 Oct 2026! Now everyone can build their own custom mala bowls right before boarding.
Credit – Mala Mia
For those of you who have never had mala before, here’s a quick guide on how to start. First, grab a bowl by the counter and head to their fridges. There, you can choose from more than 60 ingredients, including cheese, tofu and enoki mushrooms, lotus root and broccoli. With so many ingredients priced at S$2.90 per 100g, I can almost guarantee you’ll craft the perfect bowl for yourself. When you’re done, return to the counter and the staff will prepare your dish for you.
Credit – Wenwen Kee via Google
They offer a classic Stir Fry (S$1) , with options for mala or non-spicy for the quintessential mala experience. Then there’s the Mala Cream Base Dry (S$1.50) , which features a richer, unctuous flavour and slightly toned-down heat.
For something lighter and more comforting, there is their trio of soups: Chicken Collagen (S$2.50) , Mala Collagen (S$2.50) and Tomato Collagen (S$2.50) . These would be perfect right before a flight, in my opinion; they get you nice and comfy for the long ride.
Credit – foodiedoodiewoodie via Google
I think Mala Mia has done a great job catering to every kind of customer, keeping the experience casual for those who can’t really handle the spice. Also, the free-flow drinks bar for S$3.90 really helps cool things down.
There are also sides like Scrambled Egg (S$3) , Sichuan Pepper Corn Fries (S$7.90) , La Zi Ji (S$8.90) , Pao Cai (S$6.90) and Spicy Oil Dumplings (S$6.90) — p erfect bites if you aren’t too hungry or an extra for your main dish.
Credit – Zozo via Google
Also, now that it’s halal-certified, this place is an easygoing spot that anyone can go to. They were officially certified on 12 Oct 2026. If you’re like me and enjoy hanging out at Changi Airport for the ‘travel vibes’, Mala Mia is a great place to take a load off for a bite to eat.
Zi Bu Yang Sheng: Mini mala hotpot sets from $6.50 with amazing portions at Taman Jurong
summary: Mala Mia at Changi Airport Terminal 3 is a build-your-own mala outlet that opened on 14 Aug 2026 and is halal-certified. Diners pick from more than 60 ingredients, choose a dry, stir-fried or collagen soup base and set their spice level from non-spicy to extra spicy. body:
Singapore has no shortage of wine bars these days. From Champagne-only spots to natural wine bars and hotel lounges with massive wine lists, there’s plenty to choose from.
But where do people who actually spend their own money on wine like to drink?
As a member of Cat Wine Club (CWC) myself, I decided to ask fellow members to share their favourite wine bars in Singapore and why they keep going back.
These aren’t necessarily the fanciest or most expensive places. Just spots that we genuinely enjoy drinking at and would recommend to fellow wine lovers.
The list is in no particular order.
Name
Best for
Location / Area
Key highlight
Les Climats
French wine and cheese with personal recommendations
Farrer Park
French-only wine selection curated by the owner; no GST or service charge
Convivial Champagne Bar
Discovering grower Champagne beyond major labels
North Canal Road
Champagne-focused list led by an award-winning sommelier

Browsing independent wines and enjoying a glass

Casual wine shop with bottle tastings and staff recommendations

Natural wines and tasting events

temper.

Rare Burgundy and vintage Bordeaux

Over 2,000 labels; choose a bottle from the shop to drink at the bar

Premium Champagne and Burgundy for special occasions

Fine wine, rotating flights and experienced sommeliers

Over 1,000 labels, with optional membership perks

Learning about wine through guided flights

French bistro dishes, cheese boards and approachable recommendations

French wine with a full meal

Over 800 labels, a deli and a pétanque pitch
Fiasco by JUICE
Natural wine with dinner, date nights or group meals
Kampong Bugis
Independent wines and a bistro menu with Southeast Asian influences
1. Les Climats
Best for: French wine and cheese, poured by the owner himself
Les Climats in Farrer Park is a tiny 20-seater wine and cheese shop run entirely by sommelier Rajeshwaran Gopal , who previously served as group chef sommelier at Les Amis Group.
Rajesh handles everything himself, including curating the French-only wine selection, which features both established labels and lesser-known producers. The cheeses are sourced from Bernard Antony , a renowned Alsatian affineur who also supplies Michelin-starred restaurants.
One nice touch is that there’s no GST or service charge added to the bill, according to its booking listing. Quite rare for Singapore.
With just 20 seats and Rajesh personally recommending the wines, it’s a good spot if you enjoy discovering new bottles rather than just ordering something familiar off a wine list.
Wine Club Member’s Pick
“Les Climats is an awesome little wine and cheese place where i made many new discoveries which became my favourites (like after I tried egly and jessica litaud for the first time). Raj really knows how to find all the good quality plus value (he says high QPR – quality price ratio) stuff mostly from france and offers it at cost plus a small markup.”
Recommended by: Isaac
Address: 1 Tessensohn Road, #01-07, Singapore 217701
Opening hours: Mon to Fri: 3pm to 12am, Sat: 12pm to 5pm. Closed Sun
2. Convivial Champagne Bar
Credit: Convivial
Best for: Grower Champagne and getting past the big-name labels
Convivial on North Canal Road is a wine bar dedicated entirely to Champagne. Opened in 2023 by Yeo Xi Yang , winner of the 2022 Singapore National Sommelier Competition, the bar offers everything from well-known Champagne houses to smaller grower producers who make wines from their own vineyards. Xi Yang previously worked at Park90 and Les Amis, and his Champagne selection earned Convivial the Best Sparkling Wine List award from Star Wine List in 2025.
The space is fairly intimate, with arched ceilings inspired by the chalk cellars of Champagne. Even the glassware gets special attention, with handmade glasses from Czech producer Kvetna 1794. Food-wise, expect bar snacks with a local touch, including ngoh hiang , which pairs surprisingly well with Champagne.
If you’ve mostly tried mainstream Champagne labels, this is a good place to discover what smaller producers have to offer. And with an award-winning sommelier behind the bar, you can probably pick up a thing or two about Champagne while you’re at it.
Wine Club Member’s Pick
…
summary: Members of Singapore's Cat Wine Club share the wine bars they keep going back to. Expect Champagne-only Convivial, owner-run Les Climats in Farrer Park, natural wine at Temple Cellars and JUICE Wine Club in Tiong Bahru, big cellars at Park90 and temper., rare Burgundy at Patrimonio and bYU, flights at Praelum, organic French pours at Soif & Co, an 800-label French list at Le Clos and natural wine with dinner at Fiasco by JUICE. Unranked, honest and built for every budget.

Tokyo pizzeria PST serves its last pizzas at Tanjong Pagar on Saturday (31 October), 16 months after opening, CNA Lifestyle reported . Long John Silver’s at Woods Square and London Grill in Serangoon North close the same week.
PST serves its last pizzas at Tanjong Pagar on 31 October. Photo: PST
PST, Tanjong Pagar: 31 October
PST, known for its Neapolitan-style pizzas, opened at 38 Tanjong Pagar Road in June 2025. Founder-chef Tsubasa Tamaki brought the brand here on a franchise with JAP Dining Concepts, which also runs sio pasta and Sushidan.
PST broke the news in an Instagram post. A JAP spokesman described the closure as a “pause” while the team considers PST’s “next chapter” in Singapore. The team gave no specific reason, only that the decision followed “careful consideration of the team’s plans for PST Singapore and the wider dining portfolio”.
Founder-chef Tsubasa Tamaki at the PST oven. Photo: PST
The restaurant opens daily from 12pm to 3pm and 5pm to 10pm until its last day.
Long John Silver’s, Woods Square: 30 October
A notice at the Woods Square outlet in Woodlands gives 30 October as its last day of operations, The Straits Times reported . The outlet was teeming with customers at lunchtime when ST visited on 23 October, and staff there were unsure whether they would be redeployed to other outlets.
It is the latest of several closures for the chain in 2026. Its Jurong Point outlet shut on 19 October, and at least four other outlets, in Suntec City, Admiralty, Commonwealth and Tampines, closed earlier in the year. The Long John Silver’s website shows 11 outlets, down from 17 in July 2025.
Long John Silver’s current Dark Crunch menu. Photo: Long John Silver’s
London Grill, Serangoon North: 31 October
London Grill Japanese & Western at First Centre, 50 Serangoon North Avenue 4, closes for good on 31 October after 10 years, Seth Lui reported . The elderly couple who run it are retiring, with higher rent among the reasons, and have no plans to relocate.
Its prices include the Black Pepper Chicken Chop at S$6, the Chicken Burger at S$2.50, the Chicken Teriyaki Set at S$5 and the Chicken Katsu Don at S$4.30.
summary: Tokyo pizzeria PST closes at Tanjong Pagar on 31 October after 16 months, Long John Silver's shuts at Woods Square on 30 October and London Grill in Serangoon North on 31 October.
title: PST, Long John Silver’s and London Grill close their doors by 31 October

Singapore , Thailand, Indonesia… nope, UGG’s first Southeast Asia store has landed in Malaysia instead . The footwear label famous for its cosy sheepskin boots and plush slippers has officially opened its first regional store at Suria KLCC .
Credit – UGG Malaysia
Located on Level 3 of the shopping mall , the new store marks a milestone for UGG, bringing its signature blend of comfort and casual style closer to Malaysian shoppers. Known for its iconic boots, the brand has built a following among those who like their footwear to feel as good as it looks.
Credit – UGG Malaysia
Inside, you can browse the brand’s familiar favourites alongside newer designs that put fresh spins on its comfort-focused aesthetic. The store offers a chance to check out the collections in person before deciding what to bring home.
Credit – UGG Malaysia
The store carries a range of UGG footwear for men, women, and kids, including the brand’s signature Classic Mini and Ultra Mini boots , platform styles, and weather-ready designs.
Shoppers can also browse cosy slippers such as the Tasman II and Tazz II , alongside clogs and other casual footwear in colours ranging from classic chestnut and sand to black and pink.
Credit – UGG Malaysia
UGG’s appeal goes beyond keeping your toes warm, too. Its laid-back designs can be styled for casual outings or worn while lounging at home, making them versatile additions to your wardrobe.
And with the brand now having a retail space in Kuala Lumpur, fans can explore its offerings without having to rely solely on online shopping.
The opening also gives curious shoppers a chance to discover what the fuss is about, especially if UGG has been on their wish list but they have yet to try a pair for themselves.
No boarding pass needed for this UGG shopping trip. Make your way to Suria KLCC to check out the brand’s first Southeast Asia store for yourself.

body:
This is definitely not your usual chap chye (mixed vegetable rice) fare. Li Ji Cooked Food is one of the best stalls in Chinatown serving up traditional Cantonese-style dishes at super cheap prices. Some fans have noted that it’s a rare sight of homestyle cooked items in modernised Singapore.
Chinatown is home to countless famous hawker stalls. Li Ji Cooked Food is one spot that I have overlooked on too many occasions. There is always a long queue at their storefront even before the business opens. Their clientele consists mainly of old folks who crave a serving of homestyle cooked food.
The business is operated by an aunty who takes her time to dish out orders. They often sell out in 3 hours which leaves late customers to purchase from more pricey stalls in the market.
What I tried at Li Ji Cooked Food
The most popular dish was the Fish Stomach . Almost every customer ahead of me ordered at least 1 portion of this item. However, I was informed that it contained many bones. As someone who has trouble deboning fish, I gave it a miss.
Most of the dishes were unknown to me, so I relied on the recommendations from my dad. The first item that I tried was the Spicy Fermented Shrimp Paste Sliced Pork (S$1.20) . Upon the first bite, the saltiness from the pork slices shocked my palate. There was a mild spiciness but I did not expect such a strong salty flavour at all! The fermented shrimp did taste similar to har cheong gai (prawn paste chicken wings). However, I preferred the deep fried chicken wings to this saucy version.
10 best dining spots at Chinatown Point
The gravy found in this dish was too starchy for my liking. I also felt that there was nothing much to shout about from the thin pork slices used. They were tender but not mind-blowingly succulent.
The second pork item that I tried was the Sliced Pork with Sweet Preserved Vegetables (S$1.20) . The addition of preserved vegetables adequately seasoned the meat with salt. There was also a subtle sweetness and I liked the soft vegetables incorporated into the meat dish. This pork rendition was significantly less salty than the first item I tried. However, the same pork slices were used here. This meant that it was another meat dish that I did not particularly enjoy.
Another item that was a popular choice among customers was the Bittergourd (S$0.80 per slice) . Similar to the renditions found in yong tau foo stalls, the bitter vegetable was stuffed with fish paste before it was deep fried. Unfortunately, I was not content with this item, either. The vegetable was one of the most bitter that I had ever eaten. The fish paste was also not seasoned enough and did not have a distinct bouncy texture.
The last item that I added to my already-packed container was the Cabbage (S$0.70) . Seasoned with fermented beancurd, this item was the least salty of the lot. However, there was not much flavour to the dish overall. I loved the size of these cabbage pieces. They held a crunchy texture despite being cooked thoroughly. I also loved the incorporation of tofu skin and black fungus as they introduced different textures to the dish.
Final thoughts
Generally, I felt that the items sold here are acquired tastes and perhaps more familiar to the older generation. My dad expressed his disappointment towards my comments on the dishes. In his words, it was ‘too bad’ that I was not able to appreciate this authentic Cantonese cuisine. Nonetheless, the long queues in front of the stall clearly attest to its popularity. Head down to give them your support and an opportunity to try out these traditional Cantonese homestyle dishes for yourself!
People also read:
What can I do while at Chinatown in Singapore?
Which other Cantonese restaurants in Singapore do we recommend?
summary: Li Ji Cooked Food in Chinatown serves traditional Cantonese homestyle dishes at affordable prices, including fish stomach, fermented shrimp paste pork, stuffed bittergourd and cabbage. The stall attracts mainly older diners and often sells out within 3 hours, making it suited to those seeking inexpensive, traditional Cantonese fare with a queue and limited availability.
title: Li Ji Cooked Food: Affordable traditional Cantonese homestyle dishes with long history in Chinatown

body:
Geylang Serai Market and Food Centre is the heart of Singapore Malay cuisine. Many stalls there truly deserve their flowers and Pak Din Ayam Bakar is one of them.
Located on Changi Road , Geylang Serai has been an institution of Malay food for decades. Pak Din Ayam Bakar has been around for 7 years but only has 34 reviews on Google, and almost every one is positive. 7 years may not seem that long but any stall that can survive Singapore’s cutthroat food industry deserves credit.
What to order at Pak Din Ayam Bakar
While they have a few options, I decided it was best to go for their namesake: Nasi Ayam Bakar (S$7). Ayam bakar is a dish that originated during the kampung days. They would marinate the chicken in turmeric, garlic, onion paste and other spices that varied by family.
What makes it a yam bakar , however, is the fire. The name literally means ‘burnt chicken’. That’s why this dish was slightly disappointing. When it was served, the chicken was at room temperature. There was a slight smoky flavour but it was definitely missing that tell-tale char. Were it not for the kicap, the chicken would’ve been yellow from the turmeric alone.
I will say that what really makes this dish is its trio of spices — s ambal merah, sambal hijau and sambal kicap — red chilli, green chilli and sweet soya sauce. While not too spicy, these sauces added a much-needed dimension to the dish. They give notes of sweet, sour and spicy. The Neapolitan effect of the sauces also makes the plate pleasing to the eye as well as the palate.
Pergh!Chicks: Affordable Muslim-owned eatery with IG-worthy lava curry rice & ayam percik
Another dish I tried is the Rojak Bandung (S$6.50). I will admit, this is my first time trying this style of rojak. I’m more accustomed to the meaty variety of the rojak mamak and the almost-sweet freshness of Chinese rojak.
On first impression, I noticed several chunks of sliced cuttlefish, fried tofu and wilted kangkong, all of it doused in a sweet soya sauce.
This dish was actually quite surprising. The tofu had absorbed all of the sauce and was no longer crunchy. The cuttlefish didn’t really provide much flavour but instead added a chewy and bouncy texture. The kangkong added a slight bitterness and sharpness, cutting the sweet sauce.
I will say the sauce was a little too sweet for my taste. There was also a bit of spiciness, which helped balance the dish overall. While I still prefer the other 2 versions of rojak, I still found this quite pleasant. I can’t say I’d order it often, though.
Who is Pak Din Ayam Bakar best for?
If you’re looking for a quick yet satisfying meal, Pak Din Ayam Bakar is perfect for you. The food may not be my favourite but they are quick. We went up to order, waited not even 3 minutes, and the plate was already prepared.
This is likely why the chicken ended up being room temperature, as they tried to prepare the dishes ahead of time. I guess there are pros and cons to their speed. But honestly, in the hustle and bustle lifestyle of Singapore, the pros outweigh the cons.
How to get to Pak Din Ayam Bakar
There are several ways you can make your way to Geylang Serai Market and Food Centre. If you decide to take the bus, there is a bus stop opposite Geylang Serai called Joo Chiat Complex . Alternatively, there is a bus stop behind Geylang Serai called Block 416 . This is slightly further from the stall, and you would have to enter through the multi-storey carpark, so keep that in mind.
If you decide to take the MRT, your closest stop would be Paya Lebar (EW8/CC9, Green Line and Circle Line). It is around an 8-minute walk from the station. When you’ve reached the market, take note that the stalls are on the second floor, and you’ll have to go up the escalators at the centre of the building.
Also, do note that some stalls at Geylang Serai accept only cash , so make sure to have some. While Pak Din Ayam Bakar accepts PayNow, some of the drink stalls do not.
Do we recommend Pak Din Ayam Bakar?
I would recommend Pak Din Ayam Bakar. The Nasi Ayam Bakar is solid, and the prices are also fair. If the stall is not too busy, I would suggest requesting that they reheat the chicken. While it’s missing the charred flavour the dish is known for, it still is a very solid lunch. Also, the sauces really make the dish a standout.
Also, the Rojak Bandung (S$6.50) was a pleasant surprise. For that price, you can’t complain about the portions. The flavours, while slightly sweet for me, were pretty yummy. I would recommend you get it as a side if you’re feeling extra hungry.
I will say, for a store with only 34 reviews on Google, calling it a hidden gem is an understatement — speed, price and flavour are all above average. I would definitely eat here again if I’m in the area.

summary: Pak Din Ayam Bakar is a Malay stall on the second floor of Geylang Serai Market and Food Centre, serving Nasi Ayam Bakar at S$7 and Rojak Bandung at S$6.50. The grilled chicken lacked its usual char, but a trio of sambals and fast service made up for it. Best suited to anyone nearby wanting an affordable, quick Malay lunch.
title: Pak Din Ayam Bakar: Old-school ayam bakar served with a trio of sambals at this underrated stall

I seem to be on quite the roll lately in my journey through the art of Peranakan cuisine . A more refined metaphor would be to call myself a blank canvas, waiting to be painted with flavours and history. But if I’m being honest, I’m more of a Pac-Man — mouth (quite literally) open, roaming around KL and devouring everything this cuisine throws my way.
My next stop after Limapulo Terrace was The Peranakan in Bangsar — a spot boasting 4.6 stars from over 400 Google reviews (at the time of writing). They specialise in Melaka-style Peranakan cuisine, to be specific.
This particular day, I was stepping into not just one, but several new territories. Peranakan cuisine (which, truthfully, I’ve only ever dipped my toes into), Bangsar itself (a nightmare for both commuters and motorists), and the world of atas dining (well, it is Bangsar, after all). Upon arrival, I was mildly surprised to find the restaurant tucked away upstairs — a move usually reserved for indie cafes and hidden coffee spots. Hm, a curious detail worth noting.
The interior certainly leaned towards atas — though, given the price point, I’d quietly expected a touch more drama. Still, I wasn’t there to critique the decor. The real question was whether the food would make me fall head over heels for Peranakan cuisine… or send me scuttling back to safer culinary waters.
What I tried at The Peranakan
After days of eating everything but rice, my cravings finally staged a protest. And when the body calls for rice, you don’t argue. We decided to go all in with three dishes that felt like the cuisine’s greatest hits: Asam Pedas Fish (RM89) , Keluak Chicken (RM49) , and Hei Bee Eggplant (RM28) . And of course, you have to have rice with all that.
We shared a bowl of Bunga Telang Rice (RM4) — grains tinged blue from the blue pea flowers.
The Asam Pedas Fish was the first to hit the table, and immediately, a wave of sweet pineapple aroma hit me too. It was promising, but I’ll be honest — the gravy was a little thinner than I’d hoped for. The flavour leaned sweet and tangy, but the pineapple was definitely the loudest in the room, slightly overpowering other spices in the dish.
Five Sisters Nasi Lemak: Taking on Forbes’ World’s Spiciest Nasi Lemak — Carolina Reaper & Ghost Pepper sambal so hot you’ll need to sign a form
Still, the fish itself was fresh and naturally sweet, and we got 2 huge pieces of snapper , which kind of made it worth the splurge. It’s maybe not the best asam pedas I’ve ever tasted, but still enjoyable in a “I’ll definitely keep spooning more onto my plate” kind of way.
Then came the Keluak Chicken , which was packed with chicken thighs swimming in a rich, dark sauce. Imagine rendang ’s cousin who studied abroad and came back with a slightly mysterious accent — that’s this dish.
It had the same kind of depth and spice but with a distinctive earthy aftertaste from the keluak fruit. The sauce was peppery and aromatic, with a flavour that lingered in the best way. My only small gripe was that the chicken itself leaned a little firm, but nothing that ruined the overall experience.
Finally, the scene-stealer — Hei Bee Eggplant . It’s always the unassuming side dish that ends up stealing the show, isn’t it? The eggplant and green beans were charred beautifully and tossed in a shrimp paste mixture that was savoury and impossible to stop eating. I found myself wishing there was more of that magical mixture clinging to the vegetables, but even so, the dish was easily the highlight of the day.
Final thoughts
Honestly, while every dish wasn’t bad by any means, I just didn’t find myself going crazy over what The Peranakan had to offer. It’s a lovely spot for a small gathering — the food presentation is thoughtful, the ambience polished, and the service warm — but would I make a special trip all the way to Bangsar just for it? Probably not. And that’s saying something, coming from someone who has travelled over 3 hours in a day just to chase down a craving.

Pasta Bar on Keong Saik Road launches a five-course November Experience Menu on 5 November at S$88++ a person, with a minimum of two diners, on Pasta Bar’s website . The menu moves through regional Italian dishes, from the Amalfi Coast to Emilia-Romagna and Sicily.
Handmade pasta at Pasta Bar. Photo: Pasta Bar
Starters
The meal opens with three stuzzichini. A uni toast puts bafun uni on brioche with whipped brown butter and chives. Arancini come with pear mostarda and prosciutto, and gnocco fritto, the fried Italian dough, is paired with whipped feta and hot honey.
The pasta courses
• Pasta al limone: bronze die-cut eggless maccheroni with preserved lemon and pecorino romano, served in a pecorino wheel
• Tortellini in brodo: guinea fowl tortellini in consommé with pickled chayote, charred pearl onions, Thai basil, coriander and chilli sauce, a nod to Vietnamese pho
• Scoglio nero: squid ink linguine with seafood sofrito, clam jus, cockles and bincho-grilled barramundi
• Ossobuco: saffron sfoglia sheets with braised beef cheeks, bone marrow relish, shaved parmigiano and red wine jus
Pasta dishes at Pasta Bar on Keong Saik Road. Photo: Pasta Bar
The ossobuco is the kitchen’s take on the Milanese classic, with the usual saffron risotto swapped for fresh saffron pasta sheets. The pasta al limone is finished in the cheese wheel, a nod to the Amalfi Coast, where fresh lemons sit at the centre of the cooking. Scoglio, the restaurant explains, is a Southern Italian seafood dish rooted in the coastal kitchens of Campania, Puglia and Sicily.
Dessert
The fifth course is DIY cannoli. Diners fill homemade shells with sheep’s ricotta and top them with chocolate sauce, cocoa nibs, crushed pistachios and amarena cherries. Cannoli trace their origins to Sicily under Arab rule, between the 9th and 11th centuries.
A seafood pasta at Pasta Bar. Photo: Pasta Bar
Booking
Pasta Bar is at 55 Keong Saik Road, #01-05. It opens for dinner daily from 6pm to 10.30pm and for lunch from Tuesday to Saturday, 12pm to 3pm. Reservations go through the restaurant’s website, and the menu starts on 5 November.
summary: Pasta Bar on Keong Saik Road launches a five-course November Experience Menu on 5 November at S$88++ a person, from uni toast to ossobuco pasta and DIY cannoli.
title: Pasta Bar’s five-course November Experience Menu starts on 5 November at S$88++

Best hotpot buffets in Singapore
There’s no shame in admitting that cheap buffets have a chokehold on so many of us, and all the better when these affordable free-flow meals apply to hotpot experiences. Here’s a guide to the best hotpot buffets in Singapore for when you want to eat to your heart’s content without spending too much.
20 Cheap Buffets In Singapore From $7, Including Free-Flow Steak And Sashimi
1. Paradise Hotpot
Paradise Hotpot is helmed by Paradise Group, which is also behind Beauty In The Pot. Here, you can enjoy an individual hotpot buffet at wallet-friendly prices across four time slots on weekdays: early bird special (before 11:45am), lunch (11:45am to 2:30pm), tea-time (2:31pm to 4:30pm), and dinner (4:31pm to 10pm).
Prices differ according to the timeslot and protein set you choose. For example, a pork and chicken value set during the early bird and tea-time slots is priced at $20.90++ and $19.90++ respectively , while the beef and seafood premium set costs $26.90++ and $25.90++ respectively . The most expensive time to visit, of course, is during dinner, where the same sets cost $29.90++ and $38.90++ respectively. Both sets come with a soup base of your choice, with a total of eight to choose from. Some popular broths include Spicy Szechuan , Authentic Pork Bone , and Tomato with Sweet Corn . If you’re dining on a weekend, there’s a $3++ surcharge.
Read our Paradise Hotpot feature .
Website | Full list of outlets
Paradise Hotpot is not halal-certified.
Paradise Hotpot Has $18.90++ Individual Hotpot Buffet At Compass One
2. HaHaHotpot
Originally a delivery-focused service, HaHaHotpot has three outlets—Bugis, Jurong West, and Pasir Ris—offering halal hotpot buffet from only $35.90+ for weekday lunch. Choose between seven broths, including HaHa Collagen Soup , Authentic Sichuan Mala , and Seafood Soup , and a plethora of ingredients, such as Original Marinated Beef , Black Mussels , and Australian Wagyu MB4/5 Eye Round . While waiting, load up at their cooked food station, serving up local classics including Beef Rendang and Sambal Stingray .
Read our HaHaHotpot review .
Website | Full list of outlets
HaHaHotpot is halal-certified.
Is This $35.90++ Hotpot Buffet In Pasir Ris Worth Travelling For?
3. Joylion Buffet Hotpot
Image credit: Joylion Buffet Hotpot
Located at Lentor Modern and directly connected to Lentor MRT Station , Joylion Buffet Hotpot is a conveyor-belt hotpot buffet with over 100 free-flow items that come rolling right to your table. Everyone gets their own individual pot, and the belt carries premium picks such as mud crab, XL tiger prawns, fresh clams, and frog legs, alongside cooked food including hand-wrapped xiao long bao dumplings.
Their newly expanded menu gives you even more to work through. There’s now free-flow lu rou fan, spicy wonton in chilli oil, sushi, and shaker fries in cheese, chilli, and seaweed flavours. You can also craft your own bubble tea and desserts at their DIY stations. For your broth, try out their upgraded premium collagen soup base, which is now richer than before.
Lunch, from 11am to 4pm , starts from $22.90++ per person , and dinner, from 4pm to 9:30pm , starts from $32.90++ . Sauces, unlimited non-alcoholic drinks, plus over 10 varieties of desserts and fruits are all included, while soup bases cost an extra $1.80++ per diner. If one visit isn’t enough to try everything, Joylion’s recharge promotion gives you bonus dining credits when you top up:
• Silver Tier: Top up $300, get $50 free bonus credits
• Gold Tier: Top up $600, get $120 free bonus credits
• Diamond Tier: Top up $900, get $260 free bonus credits
With so much variety to go through, you’ll likely need to dine here on multiple occasions to fully savour their selection. That’s where their recharge promo will net you savings across your visits.
Make a reservation for Joylion Buffet Hotpot!
Address: 1 Lentor Central, #B1-08, Lentor Modern, Singapore 788887
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 9:30pm
Tel: 6659 1955
Website
Joylion Buffet Hotpot is not halal-certified.
4. COCA Hotpot
Thailand-famous COCA Hotpot has been in Singapore since 1987, and has earned a reputation for being the most popular Thai-Chinese hotpot restaurant. It’s located in Suntec City , serving up both weekday and weekend buffet options.
Their weekday lunch costs $39++ per person , while dinner costs $52++ . Those heading down on the weekend will have to pay $43++ during lunch, and $56++ for dinner. Though the menu differs slightly, you can expect premium ingredients at both buffets. For instance, a lunch buffet gives you access to Korean oysters , tiger prawns , and Japanese boiled scallops , whereas you can look forward to Norway salmon fillet , flower crabs, and Thai river prawns for dinner.

Cherry Garden by Chef Fei at Mandarin Oriental, Singapore has put hairy crab and Matsuba crab on its autumn menu, which runs from 1 October to 30 November 2026. The Cantonese and Teochew restaurant is serving the crab dishes in a six-course set and as à la carte plates.
The dining room at Cherry Garden by Chef Fei. Image: Mandarin Oriental, Singapore
The six-course autumn set
The autumn set costs S$288 a person, for a minimum of two diners. It opens with an appetiser trilogy of Teochew-style pork fritter, raw langoustine in garlic chilli oil with Siberian sturgeon caviar, and organic fioretto scented with wild sansho pepper.
After that come chicken consommé with fish maw and Hetian fig, braised Imperial bird’s nest with crab roe and jade melon, and crab roe xiao long bao. XO sauce stir-fried Matsuba crab with Chaoshan-style pickled vegetable and vermicelli follows, and the meal ends with double-boiled Autumn Moon pear with golden fungus and lily bulb, served with a ginger-infused crab meat pastry.
Diners can add the 15-year Shaoxing wine marinated hairy crab as a supplementary course at S$48 for half a crab or S$68 for a whole one. Availability of the hairy crab depends on supply.
Autumn dishes à la carte
Several of the autumn dishes are also sold on their own:
• 15-year Shaoxing wine marinated hairy crab, S$68 for a whole crab
• Teochew-style pork fritter, S$38 for six pieces
• Raw langoustine in garlic chilli oil with Siberian sturgeon caviar, S$108 for six pieces
• Organic fioretto scented with wild sansho pepper, S$28
• Chicken consommé with fish maw and Hetian fig, S$68
• XO sauce stir-fried Matsuba crab with Chaoshan-style pickled vegetable and vermicelli, S$288
Sautéed diced Wagyu beef with Sichuan peppercorn. Image: Mandarin Oriental, Singapore
The regular set menus
Cherry Garden’s regular sets run alongside the autumn menu. Bamboo, at S$138 a person, has a dim sum trilogy, double-boiled fish maw with scallop and matsutake, sautéed diced Wagyu beef with Sichuan peppercorn, and Yang Chun noodle with shrimp roe in chicken broth.
Lotus costs S$198, Jasmine S$218 with Xisha Island lobster in creamy garlic sauce, and Peony S$268, which includes boneless crucian carp congee.
Boneless crucian carp congee. Image: Mandarin Oriental, Singapore
Appetisers at Cherry Garden by Chef Fei. Image: Mandarin Oriental, Singapore
All prices are in Singapore dollars and subject to a 10 per cent service charge and prevailing government taxes. Cherry Garden is at Mandarin Oriental, Singapore, 5 Raffles Avenue, and takes bookings on +65 6338 0066.
summary: Cherry Garden by Chef Fei serves a six-course autumn crab set at S$288 a person, plus drunken hairy crab from S$48, until 30 November.

body:
Behind the scenes of Project Wolbachia – Singapore
Singapore recorded a 7-year low in dengue cases in 2025, with about 4,000 cases reported. This was thanks in part to residents doing their part to keep mosquito breeding at bay, alongside mosquito suppression efforts with Project Wolbachia – Singapore .
The results of Project Wolbachia have been encouraging. In Project Wolbachia release areas, Aedes aegypti mosquito populations have fallen by 80–90%, while dengue risk has been reduced by over 70%.
Today, Project Wolbachia has expanded to cover more than half of Singapore’s households, and is the first in the world to use Wolbachia suppression technology to control mosquito population in a dense, high-rise tropical city.
Behind this project is a dedicated team working tirelessly to protect communities from dengue. We had the opportunity to see how it all works:
How does Project Wolbachia actually work?
The different life stages of an Aedes aegypti mosquito.
But first, what is Project Wolbachia , and how does it actually work? Wolbachia is a naturally occurring bacterium found in more than 60% of insect species. Launched in 2016, the project breeds male Aedes aegypti mosquitoes carrying this bacterium and releases them into the community.
The Aedes aegypti mosquito is Singapore’s main dengue-spreading vector. So, the magic happens when these Wolbachia -carrying males mate with female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in the wild – the eggs produced do not hatch.
Up to twice a week, these mosquitoes are released at selected sites, which have been chosen based on factors such as historical dengue risk, and Aedes aegypti mosquito population.
Over time, the population of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in the area decreases, and in turn, dengue numbers drop too.
ICYMI, male mozzies don’t bite. And no, there is no genetic modification at work.
It all begins with gazillions of mozzie eggs
Each black dot is a mosquito egg.
But how does NEA get so many male Wolbachia -carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to constantly release into the wild? At NEA’s mosquito production facility in Ang Mo Kio, Aedes aegypti mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia are bred at scale using in-house designed technologies. Female mosquitoes naturally pass the bacterium to their offspring, enabling a steady supply of mosquitoes for the programme.
Millions upon millions of eggs are on standby at any point in time, waiting to be dipped in water and hatched.
Like a high-tech farm, but for mozzies
“These mosquitoes are highly spoiled,” we are told, and they honestly are.
Automated larvae counters. Once the eggs hatch, the larvae are counted and distributed into trays to prevent overcrowding and ensure healthy development. In the early days of Project Wolbachia , this was done manually, with staff each taking more than 3 hours to count about 4,000 larvae per tray
Today, an automated Larvae Counter can process 25,000 larvae per tray in just five minutes, dramatically increasing the programme’s production capacity.
Premium fish food is mixed with water to achieve just the right consistency and poured into automatic feeders that dispense a precise amount of food to the larvae.
The mixed feed is poured into automatic dispensers.
The conditions are optimised for them – think 28°C rooms, maintained at an ideal 80% humidity, and let’s not forget the premium feed.
Every single step of the process is painstakingly monitored and supervised; nothing is left to chance.
Going through the sorting hat
The pupae stage comes after the larvae stage, and this is where sex sorting takes place.
Loading small samples of pupae for the Pupae Size Scanner.
To ensure accurate sex separation, a sample of pupae from each batch is scanned using a Pupae Size Scanner. The separation of male and female pupae is primarily based on their size differences.
The Pupae Size Scanner measures the size distribution of male and female pupae in each batch.
The system quickly analyses pupal size distribution, allowing the team to select the optimal sieve size and minimise the chance of female pupae slipping through with the males during the sorting process.
Male pupae are smaller than female ones, so the pupae are sorted through sieves that sift out the smaller males and collect them separately.
A pupa separation system with changeable sieve sizes is used to separate the male and female pupae.
And as an added safeguard, every batch of sorted pupae undergoes low-dose X-ray irradiation to sterilise any females that may have slipped through, before release.
The most pampered mosquitoes you’ll ever meet
Then, these sorted male Aedes aegypti pupae are counted and dispensed into the lids of mosquito launchers.
The lids are attached onto the mosquito launchers, where the pupae will emerge into adult male Aedes aegypti mozzies.
Of course, the pampering doesn’t stop at the premium fish food of their baby era.
