1. The American Club
Credit – The American Club
Located at Claymore Hill near Orchard Road, The American Club is a private members’ club that combines almost everything you could ever wish for under one roof. Dining, fitness, leisure and family activities? They’ve got it all. Founded in 1948, it boasts 77 years of heritage, community and connection with generations of members. To date, there are 11,000+ members, 90+ nationalities and 25 committees at The American Club.
Credit – The American Club
Members can access various dining concepts depending on their needs. If you’re looking for something more laid-back, Central is a cafe with coffee, sandwiches and more. For something more upscale, The 2nd Floor is your best choice, featuring casual premium fine dining . Besides food, the club also offers fitness and wellness experiences . You can enjoy a multitude of sports such as Pilates, golf, swimming and squash. There is also a spa, where you can get pampered with treatments such as facials and mani-pedis to look and feel your best.

+65 6737 3411

Facebook | Instagram | Website
2. The British Club
Credit – The British Club
Want to feel as if you’re on a getaway to a secret island? The British Club is Singapore’s only Hilltop Retreat , surrounded by lush greenery. Situated in the Bukit Timah area, the club is secluded and tucked away, providing a quieter setting away from the hustle and bustle of city life. This unique club covers more than 5,900 square metres and has members of more than 50 nationalities.
Credit – The British Club
The club houses a wide variety of facilities to enjoy: 4 restaurants , 7 banquet venues , along with a range of sports and activities. Their main highlight for me has to be their 3 swimming pools ; imagine relaxing in the water whilst surrounded by all the greenery. It’s a tropical resort vacation, except you’re still in Singapore. There are 3 swimming pools for you to channel your inner Michael Phelps: a 25M main pool, a 20M lap pool and a children’s pool.

Featuring clubs across locations such as Orchard Road, Bukit Timah and the CBD, the selection caters to different lifestyles and communities. It is useful for prospective members comparing club experiences, although membership fees and application requirements should be checked directly with each club.

“You haven’t aged a day!” said no one. No one at all…
It started small. A friend I hadn’t seen in years asked if I’ve “had a rough few years.” A new colleague guessed I was in my mid-forties. I had just turned 31, thanks. Someone else ‘kindly’ said I looked “so put together for your age,” and I wasn’t sure what age they had in mind.
Life was good. I was sleeping fine, eating well, and nowhere near burnout. So why did everyone seem to be adding a few years to my look?
It wasn’t until I scrolled back through photos that it clicked. My parting had crept wider, my hairline now sits a little higher at my temples. All these changes had quietly added years to my appearance.
Hair loss is often thought of as an “older person” problem, but it doesn’t announce itself. Early hair loss and hair thinning shows up in your 20s and 30s far more often than anyone admits. A wider parting here, a fuller hairbrush there, and suddenly others realise before you do.
So I did what any curious, slightly worried person would do. I took the first step at TK TrichoKare and tried their Exosome Scalp Renewal Therapy , designed to target all types of hair loss and support fuller, thicker hair growth for S$48 nett ! Here’s how it went, and yes, the results got my attention.
Why Is My Hair Thinning So Early?
Credit: TK TrichoKare
It’s rarely just one thing, and your 20s and 30s happen to be packed with the triggers. Late nights, hormonal shifts, and constant stress can push hair out of its natural growth cycle. Hair lives in the rhythm of growing, resting, and releasing. When that quiet cycle falls out of step, or the follicle itself is inactive, the thinning starts to show. The upside is that your follicles are still very much in the game at this age, which is why acting early matters.
Catching Early Signs & Seeing What Your Mirror Can’t
Credit: TK TrichoKare
Early thinning is easy to miss, and every scalp tells a different story. That’s why the session begins with a Pre-Treatment Scan and Scalp Analysis using a Tricho-Scan device with 200x magnification . It assesses your hair density, scalp condition, and areas of concern a mirror can’t show.
Credit: TK TrichoKare
Beneath the surface of everyday routines, redness , severely clogged follicles and inflammation can quietly linger at the root. Under magnification, the scalp reveals what often goes unnoticed. These are exactly the kind of quiet issues that can disrupt growth in your 20s and 30s before visible hair loss sets in.
From here, the Hair & Scalp Specialists are able to customise treatment according to what your scalp needs.
A Herbal Scalp Reset
Credit: TK TrichoKare
Lifestyle stress and daily habits often leave the scalp oily, itchy, or inflamed, which is not a healthy base for hair growth. The treatment addresses this with a Customised European Herbal Scalp Masque , formulated with premium European Herbs and no harsh chemicals. It helps reduce excess sebum and unclog pores to support a healthier scalp environment for hair growth.
The herbal ingredients also help detoxify and soothe inflammation. Tea Tree helps relieve itching and control excess oil, while Magnolia adds shine and bounce, helps protect the hair, and soothes inflammation. .
Waking Up Tired Follicles With Exosomes
Credit: TK TrichoKare
When hair fall becomes visible, a targeted routine makes all the difference. That’s where the Exosome serum comes in. It’s sprayed evenly onto the scalp, then TrichoKare’s OxyJet Infusion takes over. Using a gentle, pressurised stream of oxygen, the OxyJet opens up tiny pathways in the skin so the serum can travel deeper, right down to the hair follicles where it’s needed most.
The oxygen does more than just open the door – it also energises the follicles for healthier growth and renewal, while helping to protect them from the damage caused by stress. This simple 2-step approach ensures the exosomes are absorbed far more effectively than they would be on the surface alone. Your specialist then massages everything in, helping to repair and awaken weaker follicles, for stronger, thicker hair over time.
Keeping The Growth Phase Going with Low Light Therapy
Credit: TK TrichoKare
Many people don’t realise how important it is to keep the scalp’s pH in balance. Low-light Therapy features a device designed to balance the scalp’s pH level. It prolongs the growth phase while reducing inflammation that disrupts growth, and improves blood flow and delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the hair roots.
The Proof Is In The Scalp
Credit: TK TrichoKare
The big reveal of results can feel scary. But fret not! The Post-Treatment Scalp Scan Analysis is calm, clear, and walks through with you every step of the way, with a side-by-side comparison up close, from where you started to where you are now.
Similarly, a Tricho-Scan device with 200x magnification will be used to see magnified evidence of a healthier scalp from just one session of Exosome Scalp Renewal Therapy.

body:
Things Singaporeans used to do the analogue way
As millennials, looking at trends from 2006 coming back and the younger generation calling them “vintage” now is a humbling reminder of our age. And in Singapore too, some things we used to do feel almost prehistoric now. Think tearing paper parking coupons, standing by the roadside trying to flag a cab, or carrying cash around just in case a shop didn’t accept cards. Back then, these were simply a part of everyday life.
Fast-forward to 2026, and technology has quietly taken a lot of that friction out of our routines. From ride-hailing apps and digital payments to biometric immigration clearance when we travel, plenty of things we once did manually can now be sorted with a few taps on a screen. Here are some everyday things Singaporeans used to do the analogue way – and how tech has made life a whole lot easier since.
1. Getting passport stamps
Now: Passportless immigration clearance
Image credit: @anders.jpg via Instagram
Remember when going overseas meant handing your passport over at immigration and waiting for that satisfying chop? Passport stamps were practically souvenirs in themselves – frequent travellers could flip through the pages and get a little visual recap of everywhere they’d been.
These days, though, clearing immigration at Changi Airport is much more seamless. Since September 2024, passportless clearance has been fully rolled out across all four4 terminals, allowing Singapore residents to clear immigration using facial and iris biometrics instead of physically presenting their passports. Foreign visitors can also use passportless clearance when departing Singapore.
Image credit: Now Boarding by Changi Airport
Cameras at the automated lanes scan your face and irises and match them against your registered identity, so your biometrics can be used to verify your identity without you having to physically present your passport at the counter. In fact, ICA says the average immigration clearance time has dropped from 25 seconds to just 10 seconds per traveller, cutting it by about 60%. Super impressive, isn’t it?
That’s a pretty big upgrade from digging around your bag for your passport while panicking about holding up the queue behind you. But don’t get too carried away with the “passportless” part. You’ll still need to bring your physical passport along for travel, since other countries may require it and ICA can still ask for it for verification.
2. Flagging taxis by the side of the road
Now: Ride-hailing apps
Image credit: Wikimedia Commons
Before ride-hailing apps became second nature, getting a cab could feel like a mini mission. You either had to flag one down by the roadside, head to a taxi stand, or call for a booking. And all of those options still depended on whether there was an available cab nearby. You also had to consider peak hour, heavy rain, or a driver changing shift.
Now, most of that happens quietly in the background. Ride-hailing apps use GPS and real-time data to match you with a nearby driver, show you the fare upfront, and let you track the car as it makes its way over.
You can book your car while sitting at home watching Netflix as you wait for it to arrive. You can also see your driver and vehicle details before getting in, and pay in-app without having to prepare cash. So, instead of physically hunting for transport, we now just watch a tiny car icon inch closer on a map.
It’s one of those everyday conveniences that barely feels high-tech anymore – until you remember how much more effort catching a cab used to take.
3. Buying DVDs & CDs
Now: Streaming services like Netflix, Disney Plus or HBO
Image credit: Ong Rui En
There used to be a whole ritual involved in watching a movie or listening to an album. You’d head to a DVD or CD shop , hunt down the title you wanted, buy or rent it, then make sure you actually had the right player at home. And once your collection started growing, there was the very real problem of figuring out where to store all those discs.
Image credit: Tagvenue
Streaming did away with most of that hassle. Platforms like Netflix, Disney+, and HBO let us access huge libraries of shows and movies almost instantly, while music streaming services put millions of songs on the same phone we already carry around every day. You don’t have to invest in a separate player or dig through a stack of cases to find the one movie you feel like watching.
The technology behind streaming – things like cloud storage and high-speed internet – may be doing a lot of work in the background. But the lifestyle upgrade is simple: entertainment went from something we had to physically own and organise to something we can pull up with a few taps.
4. Shopping at traditional staffed stores
Now: Unmanned/AI-powered supermarkets
…
summary: From passport chops to paper parking coupons, these 7 everyday things Singaporeans used to do the analogue way now take just a few taps.
title: 7 Things Singaporeans Used To Do The Analogue Way That Feel Ancient In 2026

body:
Defence Collective Festival 2026
The Defence Collective Festival (DCF) is back! This year’s edition marks the 2nd run of this annual event, with last year’s marking both SG60 and SAF60. If you missed it in 2025, or didn’t get enough of the festivities, it’s happening again this 14th to 15th November 2026 , 10am to 6pm , at Singapore Discovery Centre , Singapore Navy Museum , and Singapore Air Force Museum .
It’s a new year, new wow, because this year’s edition is packed with loads of fun activities, which we got a taste of at Singapore Discovery Centre – each of the 3 museums has its own special line-up of activities, so you’ll have to visit them all to try everything. Here are some of the highlights that you can look forward to:
How much are tickets?
Before we get into the activities, you might ask – how much are the tickets? The good news is that admission to the Defence Collective Festival is free .
However, you have the option to purchase a Premium: Exclusive Passport ($10) to take part in any of the Premium activities . You can do this online at the Defence Collective Festival website , or on-site at any of the museums, on both days of the festival. Yes, the passport is valid at all 3 museums and covers the whole weekend.
Plus, Exclusive Passport holders get to take home a Defence Collective Festival tote bag .
Try your hand at gel blaster shooting
We foresee that the Target Lane Shooting at Singapore Discovery Centre will be a super hot activity. You’ll be different types of gel blasters, loaded up with gel bullets, and tasked to shoot at targets. The targets are set at varying distances for shooters of all levels, so everyone can join in on the fun. Do note that younger participants will need to be accompanied by an adult.
Crack riddles in a gallery that’s “come alive”
The 2nd Premium activity at the Singapore Discovery Centre takes interactive mystery-solving to the next level. Enter their galleries, Through The Lens Of Time and Sandbox to take a walk through Singapore’s history, and solve the riddles in your passport.
P.S. Each museum has their own take on this activity, so try them all!
Once you’ve solved the riddles, look for the labelled cardboard boxes in the galleries, and seek out the secret password , which you’ll have to give to the characters there.
You’ll have to give the right password to the characters, including a Samsui woman and a Phua Chu Kang lookalike, to get a stamp in your passport.
There are 4 characters whom you’ll meet in the gallery, but don’t worry, you don’t need all 4 stamps to complete this activity. Just 2 will do.
Pilot a drone at “sea”
Image for illustrative purposes only.
Image credit: Defence Collective Singapore
At the Singapore Navy Museum, Reach & Rescue gives you the chance to operate a drone through a maritime course, collecting aid packages, dodging obstacles, and delivering supplies to the right rescue point before time runs out.
Become a human claw machine
Image for illustrative purposes only.
Image credit: Defence Collective Singapore
Meanwhile, at the Air Force Museum, there’s the Air Supply Mission , which turns you into a human claw machine, gathering supplies and delivering them to your intended destination.
Take part in free activities across all 3 museums
If you’re not getting the passport, fret not, because there are free activities aplenty at all of the museums for participants of all ages.
For those of you who are holding the passport, follow the instructions in your passport on the Fringe Activities page to collect more stamps!
Think like a tactical ops engineer
Think like a tactical ops engineer and beat the clock to build a bridge across the river – just like in the field. You’ll have to avoid the obstacles, and use only the tools that you’re provided.
Decode a Morse signal
Then, send a Morse message to your friend, using just a torchlight. Pay attention, because short and long flashes mean totally different things!
Crack codes to solve puzzles
Put your best spy cap on too – there’s puzzle-solving to do, and no time to lose. You’ll have to crack the codes to put the clues together, and solve the puzzle before the clock runs out.
Step into the shoes of a first responder
Image credit: Defence Collective Singapore
There is an entire force of first responders who are always on standby for any emergencies that may crop up in Singapore, and at SDCity , a Singapore Discovery Centre-exclusive activity, the little ones will get a chance to step into the shoes of these frontliners.
Don a firefighting suit, paramedic outfit, or policeman uniform, get in your vehicle, and go on duty around the miniature city to put out all the fires in town.
Build a city & make a pledge to Singapore’s defence
Little hands can make a difference too, and at Dream City Builder , they’re literally the architects of a tabletop city that they put together, brick by brick.
…
summary: The Defence Collective Festival returns on 14th-15th Nov 2026 with free activities across 3 museums, plus a $10 passport for gel blaster shooting, drone flying and more.
title: Defence Collective Festival 2026 Has A Human Claw Machine, Drone Flying & Gel Blaster Battles Across 3 Museums

Odette sits at No. 15 on The 50 Best Restaurants 2026 list, the only Singapore restaurant inside the top 50 . The ranking came out at the awards ceremony in Lima, Peru, on 4 November 2026.
Chef Julien Royer is on the pass at the modern French restaurant in National Gallery Singapore. Pastry chef Louisa Lim is named on the same official profile. The list, formerly The World’s 50 Best Restaurants, is organised by British media group William Reed and was rebranded in September 2026.
Head sommelier Lesley Liu takes Best Sommelier
Odette’s head sommelier, Lesley Liu, won the Best Sommelier Award 2026 , sponsored by Vik. She works alongside wine director Vincent Tan on a cellar of more than 1,000 bottles, with a list focused on terroir and craft, unconstrained by price, region or style.
Liu joined Odette after earlier posts in Taichung and Shanghai, and holds professional credentials from the Wine & Spirit Education Trust and the Association de la Sommellerie Internationale.
Lesley Liu won the Best Sommelier Award 2026. Image: The 50 Best Restaurants
Three more Singapore names on 51 to 100
Singapore also holds three places on the extended 51 to 100 list , released earlier:
• Seroja at Duo Galleria, Fraser Street: No. 64, a new entry. Chef Kevin Wong’s 24-seat room focuses on Malay Archipelago cooking.
• Burnt Ends: No. 89. Chef Dave Pynt’s smokehouse cooks over a custom dual-cavity oven and elevation grills.
• Labyrinth: No. 98. Chef Han Liguang (LG Han) plates progressive Singaporean cooking built on local flavours.
Odette’s dining room at National Gallery Singapore. Image: Odette
Where Odette sits
Odette opened in 2015 and runs at 1 St Andrew’s Road, #01-04 National Gallery Singapore. Royer sources from artisanal producers in Asia and Europe for French fine dining with Asian-inspired flourishes, and Dawn Ng’s paper sculpture hangs behind the host station.
Spain’s Asador Etxebarri took No. 1. Bookings and current menus sit on Odette’s own site .
A plated course at Odette. Image: Odette
summary: Odette is No. 15 on The 50 Best Restaurants 2026, the only Singapore entry in the top 50. Head sommelier Lesley Liu won Best Sommelier, with Seroja, Burnt Ends and Labyrinth on 51 to 100.
title: Odette at No. 15 on The 50 Best Restaurants 2026, with Lesley Liu Best Sommelier

Readers living in Punggol , especially Northshore, rejoice! FoodHub in Northshore Plaza I opened its doors on 6 Nov 2026 . The food court is located at #01-08/18 , directly opposite Koi and beside Giant. With 14 stalls under 1 fully air-conditioned roof, the residents get more food options.
To celebrate its opening, diners can get 80c Kopi O or Teh O for just 80 cents . There will also be budget meals such as traditional breakfasts for S$2.50. In this economy? Yes please.
Those residing nearby may know that there are many vacant stalls around Northshore Plaza, but the mall seems to be undergoing a revival with new food stalls. One of those is Hippopotato , which opened in Oct 2026. This new FoodHub is an addition to the food scene — the mall previously only had 1 food court — Bagus by Kopitiam.
Do note that some of the stalls were not operating when I visited on the morning of 6 Nov 2026, but they are expected to open within the next few days. Without further ado, here are the stalls available and some dishes you can savour.
Let’s start off on the left side of FoodHub. First, you’ll be greeted by a chain brand — Yuen Kee Dumpling . They serve dumplings and wantons with fillings such as pork and tobiko . There’s also Thai Tze Char , which sells Chicken Wing Rice (S$3) .
If you’re like me and can’t eat a meal without a drink, head to the Beverages & Desserts stall . Drinks , including Iced Calamansi start from S$2.10 . The Chicken Rice stall right beside the Beverages & Desserts stall offers Roasted / Steamed Chicken Rice at S$4.50 .
For those who love noodles, Wen Ji Noodle sells a variety of noodles starting from S$3 . You can’t go wrong with their signature Dry / Soup Fishball Noodle (S$5.60) . If you prefer duck over chicken, make a beeline for Taste Legend Charcoal Roasted Delights , with dishes such as Boneless Duck Rice (S$4) and Boneless Duck Noodles (S$5.50) .
Veggie lovers can try out Yuan Yang Spinach Soup , offering Spinach Sliced Food Porridge (S$6.50) and Spinach Seafood Soup (S$5.50) amongst others. You’ll be sure to have a warm, comforting meal at Ling Nan Claypot , where prices start at S$5.80 .
Get your mala fix at Wonderful Mala Hotpot ; ingredients are priced at S$2.28/100g — affordable in my opinion. Do note that there’s a minimum order value of S$7. Ruchulu declares itself the House of Flavours for South and North Indian food as well as Indo-Chinese delights.
For those who love Korean and Japanese cuisine, there’s a fusion stall you won’t want to miss. Choose from their range of bentos, curry rice and noodles . There’s even Fat Beef Sukiyaki (S$8.80) . Abang Gemuk sells mouth-watering burgers, Western grill, pasta, rice and finger foods starting at S$3.
844 Prawn Noodle has Sliced Pork Bee Hoon Soup for S$3 , while its prawn dishes start at S$6. It’s not a food court without the shiny caifan stall; the Mixed Vege stall sells a combination of 2Veg 1Meat for just S$3 .
10 best hawker stalls at the all-new One Punggol Hawker Centre you need to know about
summary: FoodHub at Northshore Plaza I in Punggol opened on 6 Nov 2026, bringing 14 stalls under 1 air-conditioned roof. Residents can find affordable meals ranging from S$2.50 traditional breakfasts and S$3 chicken wing rice to dumplings, noodles, claypot dishes, mala and Indian cuisine. With budget-friendly options and a variety of cuisines, it is a convenient addition for Northshore residents seeking more dining choices.

body:
Roaming the busy streets of Jalan Besar, I tend to pass by restaurants with claims like ‘Best’ or ‘Ultimate’. Bismillah Biryani on Dunlop Street is one of the unique cases where those claims are backed up. A spot that boasts 9 Michelin Bib Gourmands. If that is somehow not impressive enough for you, they have had those Bib Gourmands every year since 2016 (except for 2020 due to COVID) . Biryani is also arguably the most popular indian dish in Singapore, so I obviously assume one bite of their biryani will blow my socks clean off.
To those wondering, ‘what’s the big deal about the Bib Gourmand thing?’ Well, the Michelin Bib Gourmand recognises not just how good the food is, but also the quality, value and the bar of that recognised dish. In this case, it is the biryani. So let’s see how good their biryani really is.
When we entered the restaurant, my friends and I noticed the condition of the place. The tables were shaky and overlapped. The windows were stained, and not in the intentional way; it has a very old-school charm about it. The entire spot just screams ‘no nonsense.’ You’re there for the biryani and nothing else. I respect that, to be honest.
What to order at Bismillah Biryani
We wasted no time ordering. I had several Michelin-recognised meals in my life, and I was relatively confident I could determine if it was truly worth the recognition. We order the Lamb Shank Biryani (S$28.50 à la carte, S$32.90 for the set). We elected to order the set, which includes 1 samosa, a bowl of aloo mattar and a mango lassi. We also ordered an extra side of Samosas (S$4.50 for 3) and Pista Kulfi (S$4.90) as it was unbelievably hot that day.
Let’s start with the starter. The Samosas (S$4.50 for 3) were absolutely classic. The crust was thick and buttery with a slight saltiness. So many spots that serve samosas neglect the crust, often tasting bland despite the nice texture. Bismillah Biryani does not. The filling was nicely seasoned, with the taste of cumin, and the spice was just right. However, I love my food spicy, so do be careful should you order this.
What really levels up this treat is the mint sauce. It was bright, smooth and refreshing. It made each bite of the samosa very balanced, as well as cutting through the richness. Don’t have it without the sauce.
Singapore’s highest-rated biryani has 4.9 stars — is it really that good?
Now onto the main event. The Lamb Shank Biryani (S$28.50 à la carte) is, unfortunately, quite disappointing. I’ll start with the positives. The lamb shank was wildly tender. While trying to get a pick-up shot with the fork, the meat pretty much unravels. It was juicy, fatty and soft. However, I do wish the shank overall was seasoned better.
There was also a side of Aloo Mattar that came with the set. It was spicy with a smoky curry flavour. The potatoes were fluffy and stewed in the curry very well. I could taste the fragrant curry throughout the surprisingly chunky potato. It added a much-needed contrast to the rice.
And therein lies the problem. The rice has all the telltale signs of a beautiful biryani . The grains were nice and separated. It was firm but not hard. The colour is what you’d expect from North Indian biryani. Slightly pale but fragrant. North Indian biryani is supposed to be milder and floral compared to the more common biryani, which is heavily spiced and rich. The rice was anything but mild.
Biryani experts would be familiar with biting into one of the cloves when eating the rice. That sudden shock of spice acts like a flashbang to the senses. Now, imagine that, but the entire time you’re eating. I will say, alongside the Aloo Mattar and lamb shank, the rice started to balance out. But I won’t lie, that was a wild first impression.
On the brighter side, the p ista kulfi (S$4.90) and mango lassi were delightful. Kulfi is a South Asian ice cream that uses highly reduced, unsweetened condensed milk as the dairy of choice. It is sweet, rich and carries flavour surprisingly well. In this case, it’s blessed with the nutty notes of pistachio. The mango lassi is also brilliant. That sweet, illuminating mango flavour along with the tart and rich yoghurt was a match made in heaven. With the day being as hot as it was, these two items saved my friend and me. No, I’m not exaggerating.
Who is Bismillah Biryani best for?
I will say, there is a chance that this was a bad batch. I can only say for certain if I come over again another time. But even then, I still feel that this biryani is nothing mind-blowing, and not something you would expect from a restaurant that has received the Michelin Bib Gourmand 9 times. But if you’re just looking for a decent biryani with some pretty awesome sides, I’d say give Bismillah Biryani a shot.
Also, I do notice a lot of younger patrons trying out the dishes and taking loads of pics. I feel like this place is definitely a hotspot for those foodies who enjoy testing whatever is reported to be the best.
How to get to Bismillah Biryani
…
summary: Bismillah Biryani on Dunlop Street in Jalan Besar is a Michelin Bib Gourmand holder serving lamb shank biryani from S$28.50. The shank is tender, but cloves dominate the rice, while the samosas, aloo mattar and pista kulfi stand out. Best suited to diners curious about Michelin-recognised biryani who go in with realistic expectations.
title: Bismillah Biryani: Is this 9x Michelin Bib Gourmand really that good?

Fans of Initial D might recognise the familiar look of Fujiwara Tofu Shop at first glance, but this Johor Bahru newcomer has a few surprises up its sleeve.
Credit – Yucee Cafe
Yucee Cafe in Permas City , JB takes inspiration from the iconic anime, though you won’t find the usual tofu shop menu here. Instead of sticking to traditional tau fu fah , it puts a creative spin on the humble soy dessert, with a cafe by day and bar by night concept to round things off.
Credit – Yucee Cafe
Forget the typical brown sugar syrup and taro balls, this cafe experiments with flavours such as crème brûlée , black sesame and matcha . One creation worth checking out is TauFuFaaaaa , which swaps the usual sugary toppings for a lightly savoury milk foam and a drizzle of honey.
Credit – Yucee Cafe
There’s a reason to visit even if tofu pudding isn’t your thing. During the day, Yucee Cafe serves coffee and matcha for those who fancy a slow afternoon, while evenings bring out its bar side, with cocktails, mocktails and house-made drinks.
Credit – Yucee Cafe
Going with a group? Get the 6-glass cocktail set , which works out to around RM19.70 per glass . You can mix and match flavours, even throw in a mystery drink, and save any unfinished drinks for your next visit.
Credit – Yucee Cafe
Beer lovers can also try locally crafted brews by KL-based Monster & Beer , featuring tropical fruit-forward flavours and varying alcohol strengths rather than the usual bitter profiles.
Yucee Cafe in JB brings together a little bit of nostalgia, a playful take on traditional tau fu fah and a cafe-bar concept that gives you a reason to visit at different times of the day. Even if you’re not an Initial D fan, the unique tofu choices and vibes alone make for a fun change worth adding to your itinerary.
Gosame KL: We tried Seoul’s famous grilled mackerel & spicy squid everyone’s talking about
summary: Yucee Cafe in Permas City, Johor Bahru, takes inspiration from Initial D while giving traditional tau fu fah a creative twist with flavours such as crème brûlée, black sesame and matcha. Its cafe-by-day, bar-by-night concept also offers coffee, matcha, cocktails and locally crafted Monster & Beer brews, making it a suitable spot for dessert lovers and groups looking to share a six-glass cocktail set at around RM19.70 per glass.
title: This new Initial D-inspired Fujiwara Tofu Shop cafe in JB serves unique tau fu fah, matcha & cocktails

Matchaya is taking 30 per cent off its Cloud Series kakigori at the Tiong Bahru flagship until 22 November 2026. The five bowls are exclusive to 82 Tiong Poh Road, #01-05 , and the Tiong Bahru menu prices them from S$18++ to S$22++ before the discount.
The line is part of Matchaya 3.0, under the name The Cloud Series. The ice is made by Kuramoto Ice in Kanazawa, Japan, and sourced through Kuramoto Ice Singapore, a family trade the brand traces to 1923. Each bowl is shaved into layers of sauce, cream and texture on that ice.
Five flavours on the Cloud Series
Five bowls sit on the kakigori menu, all marked as a Tiong Bahru exclusive:
• Signature Koicha Azuki: S$22++. Ceremonial matcha with azuki, red kidney beans, house-made granola and a delicate milk cream espuma.
• Burnt Butter Houjicha: S$18++. Roasted houjicha with brown butter cream, brown sugar jelly and a spiced Biscoff crumble.
• Chocolate Tiramisu: S$18++. Rich chocolate, ladyfingers and mascarpone cream with cacao chips, served alongside a double shot of espresso.
• Mango Coconut: S$20++. Mango compote and coconut cream espuma, with dried coconut and mango popping boba.
• Strawberry Yogurt: S$20++. Strawberry compote and fresh strawberries, with a tangy yogurt espuma and berry crisps.
Menu prices are subject to a 10 per cent service charge and GST. Matchaya’s homepage lists kakigori at 30 per cent off until 22 November. It does not set out further terms, so check in store before ordering.
How the bowls are built
Signature Koicha Azuki stacks koicha sauce with azuki paste and homemade matcha granola, then a Hokkaido milk espuma finished with koicha powder and red kidney beans.
Matchaya’s layer diagram for Signature Koicha Azuki. Image: Matchaya
Burnt Butter Houjicha holds houjicha sauce, brown sugar jelly and Biscoff crumble under a brown butter cream and a Hokkaido milk espuma. Chocolate Tiramisu uses a 73 per cent dark chocolate sauce with chocolate chips, ladyfingers and mascarpone cheese, and comes with a double shot of espresso on the side.
Matchaya’s layer diagram for Chocolate Tiramisu. Image: Matchaya
Strawberry Yogurt builds homemade strawberry sauce, strawberry compote, freeze-dried strawberry crumble and strawberry konjac balls under a yogurt espuma with lemon zest. Mango Coconut pairs mango sauce and mango compote with toasted coconut flakes and mango popping boba, then a coconut espuma with lemon zest and diced mango.
Matchaya’s layer diagram for Burnt Butter Houjicha. Image: Matchaya
Only at the Tiong Bahru flagship
The Tiong Bahru tea bar opens daily from 9.30am to 9.30pm. Havelock MRT is 7 minutes away, Outram 9 minutes and Tiong Bahru 13 minutes.
Matchaya’s menu marks the kakigori as a Tiong Bahru exclusive, and notes that the bowls are best enjoyed immediately.
summary: Matchaya is taking 30 per cent off its five Cloud Series kakigori bowls at Tiong Bahru until 22 November. Menu prices run from S$18++ to S$22++ before the discount.

Tucked away in a corner of the Seksyen 14’s Medan Ria food court sits a noodle stall, still and pristine. Behind the noodle stall sits an 84 year-old man, eager for the lunch crowd to arrive.
Since the 1970s, Lum Kee Laksa has been serving different types of laksa to the people of Petaling Jaya. This humble stall specialises in only 4 dishes: asam laksa , Siam laksa , curry laksa , and prawn noodles .
Their Halal certificate is displayed at the stall’s window, so don’t worry.
The moment we approached the stall, the owner greeted us and promptly explained his menu, telling us that most patrons come for his curry laksa . Oh, we were even more eager now to try.
What I tried at Lum Kee Laksa
Visually, their Asam Laksa (RM9 for small) is your standard sweet and spicy noodle dish. The broth was a deep reddish brown and the laksa noodles a milky white, topped with a fresh mix of cucumber, onions, pineapple, mint leaves, and sliced chillies. There was plenty of shredded fish in the bowl to get that full bite.
As a big fan of asam laksa , I was ready for the familiar sour and spicy kick to envelope my taste buds. However, my first sip of broth was dominantly savoury. I tilted my head in mild confusion as I scooped another spoonful of fish soup. Same thing. It was missing the strong tanginess I associate with asam laksa , as the first word in the dish’s name suggests.
This could be attributed to the shrimp paste that was already on the spoon when served to me. Without a second thought, I mixed everything in to meld the flavours together. The saltiness of the shrimp paste could have overpowered the tang of the broth.
The laksa noodles were perfectly cooked, as expected from someone who had been manning his own stall for around 40 years. They were springy and soft, allowing for a delightful chewing experience.
Moving on to the Curry Laksa (RM9 for small) , the curry taste was quite mild. The santan made for an extremely creamy and smooth broth, but flavour-wise, it didn’t pack a punch. This curry laksa is perfect for those who can’t tolerate spice, as this dish wasn’t spicy, even after mixing in the sambal .
The stall is generous with their toppings of sliced fish cakes, tofu , and green beans.
Sisters Place: Kopitiam serving authentic halal Chinese dishes like CKT, Hokkien mee & yee mee
One thing that sets Lum Kee Laksa apart from other noodle stalls is their cockles— look at how huge they were! Certainly double or triple the size of the ones you’d find in your usual plate of char kuey teow .
When asked about it, the owner said that these cockles were difficult to source, making his stall special. The cockles start off pretty mellow when you first bite into them, and then the brininess hits after you’ve chewed for a bit.
Much like the previous dish, the yellow noodles of the curry laksa were well cooked. They did have that slight aftertaste— as Malaysians call it, the kapur or chalky aftertaste. Thankfully, it wasn’t too prominent and I could easily get past it.
Final thoughts
As someone who loves strong, intense flavours, this stall didn’t really hit the spot. It is, however, perfect for those who like more calm and mild flavours. While the asam laksa and curry laksa were not as satisfying as I had hoped, I can understand why locals have been frequenting Lum Kee Laksa for decades. The food tastes homemade and exudes comfort. Even the food court feels nostalgic; it’s a good break from the modern, minimalist eateries of today.

summary: Lum Kee Laksa in Petaling Jaya’s Medan Ria food court is a long-running stall known for serving asam laksa, curry laksa, Siam laksa and prawn noodles, prepared by its 84-year-old owner. The review focuses on flavour and texture, noting mild, comforting broths, generous toppings and unusually large cockles, with dishes priced from RM9. Best suited for diners who prefer gentle, home-style laksa over bold or spicy flavours, especially those seeking a nostalgic, halal option in Seksyen 14.

I’m constantly searching for authentic restaurants to satisfy my Korean food cravings. I love classic bibimbap as well as spicy and cheesy tteokbokki , but nothing beats a decent Korean BBQ.
Fellow Korean food lovers, here’s a list of 22 Korean BBQ restaurants in Singapore that you should try at least once to satisfy that K-BBQ fix!
How I chose these best Korean BBQ restaurants
These are the 3 main criteria I used to decide which restaurants to recommend:
• Quality: The restaurants on this list are known for high-quality food that offer good value for money.
• Service : True to Korean dining fashion, the staff offer attentive and friendly service.
• Ambience : Beyond good food, the restaurants here have a comfortable and inviting atmosphere.
I have also grouped them into 2 different categories, so you can find what suits you best.
• À la carte
• Buffets
This isn’t a ranked best-to-worst Korean BBQ restaurants list, but a collection of the most enjoyable ones overall, in no particular order.

1. Seorae Jib
With 4 outlets across Singapore, Seorae Jib celebrates 10 years of Authentic Korean Culinary Craftsmanship by providing premium charcoal K-BBQ experiences.
Besides the 100 Knife Cuts Kkot Samgyeobsal , the chefs at Seorae Jib also apply a precision ‘accordion-fold’ technique to the Dwaeji Galbi (marinated pork collar) to help the marinade penetrate more thoroughly and enhance its tenderness. Carefully angled cuts on each side allow the pork collar to fan out like an accordion. The result? Flavourful and soft meat that makes you go back for seconds.
Tired of festive turkeys and ham for your Christmas celebrations? Then switch things up, gather 1 or 2 friends, and enjoy The Christmas Grill (S$128++) . Besides your choice between the 100 Knife Cuts Kkot Samgyeobsal and Dwaeji Galbi , the set includes the Xmas-exclusive Red Wine Infused Buchaesal . Each bite of this top blade cut beef releases rich, wine-kissed nuances that make each piece enticing.
You’ll also get to indulge in the Signature Galmaegisal (pork skirt), Spicy Dakgalbi (chicken), and your choice of Jjigae — Kimchi , Sundubu , or Doenjang .
In honour of their 10th anniversary, Seorae Jib is offering a delicious Jeju Pork Platter (S$59). Sourced from Jeju Island, this meat is prized for its natural marbling and buttery richness. Enjoy a ‘Wagyu of Pork’ experience with the Pork Collar , Loin , Belly , and Tenderloin ,

body:
For the past few months, I have eaten at possibly every OG chicken rice stall in KL and Selangor . But it’s always been the same ol’ roast chicken. So you can imagine my surprise when I came across Gerai Ah Kow , a halal chicken rice stall in KL serving Horlicks sesame fried chicken! Yes, HORLICKS! Of course, I had to check out this unique dish.
Situated inside Medan Selera Jalan Raja Muda Abdul Aziz (opposite Hospital Besar Kuala Lumpur). If you’re able to find a parking space during lunch time, then you truly have lady luck by your side.
Fun fact, this stall has been around since 1983. Ah Kow came up with the ingenious sesame chicken recipe and has since passed it down to his son, Eric and son in law, Kenny.
What I tried at Gerai Ah Kow
I ordered the Horlicks Sesame Fried Chicken (RM16) , Rice (RM2.50) and a plate of Bean Sprouts (RM7) . Keep in mind that Gerai Ah Kow practices self-service so you’ll have to patiently wait for the ladies to place your order on a tray before you can find a table and tuck in. I didn’t mind this one bit, after all good things come to those who wait!
Horlicks sesame fried chicken aside, this was your typical chicken rice spread— rice, a bowl of soup, chilli sauce. The chicken slices are served on a bed of sliced cucumbers bathed in light soya sauce and topped with coriander.
I’ll be honest. I really didn’t expect anything out of the fried chicken albeit the rave reviews— it’s fried chicken, it’s already tasty, how could it possibly get any better? Boy, was I absolutely wrong.
A bite of the fried chicken skin and I was ready to call everyone on my contact list to try it out too. The beautiful golden skin was unbelievably loaded with crunch. The crispy fried chicken crust cracked with every bite… and I was hooked. I just wanted more of that brown crispy skin peppered with sesame seeds. And the goodness doesn’t stop there. The white flesh underneath was so succulent and I found myself mechanically just reaching for more of the utterly delicious chicken.
Sisters Place: Kopitiam serving authentic halal Chinese dishes like CKT, Hokkien mee & yee mee
Yes, the chicken was perfection on its own but the spicy chilli sauce (be warned those who can’t take heat) just elevated the flavours even more. I also suggest you order the bean sprouts— they were definitely the underdog dish on the menu. They were fresh, fat and crunchy— after all bean sprouts grown in Ipoh are the best in the world!
If there was a pedestal dedicated to fried chicken, this Horlicks Sesame Fried Chicken would be adorned with jewels. Sorry, Uncle Lim .
Frankly, the rice and soup were nothing to shout about but were the ideal supporting crew to the chicken. Also, if you’re wondering whether or not the taste of Horlicks was overpowering, I’m happy to report that it is not. I also found out that the addition of Horlicks lends to the crispy texture of the fried chicken and the sesame seeds adds a nutty crunch. The best part was that after the entire meal, I noticed something very apparent— itI didn’t leave that usual greasy, fried chicken aftertaste. Bonus!
Final thoughts
“I’m going to tapau another two packets of fried chicken. Do you want me to get you a packet?” suggested my companion who couldn’t stop cooing about how delicious the chicken was.
I laughed. And said yes. How could I not share this delightful find with my loved ones— that would be plain evil. Plus, I was so curious to know if the fried chicken would still retain its crunchy texture.
As I watched my friend place her takeaway order, I noticed that almost everyone sitting in the food court was tucking into the chicken rice. There were plenty of other stalls but Gerai Ah Kow is undoubtedly in a league of its own.
A bite of the Horlicks Sesame Fried Chicken is worth every second in traffic and hours spent searching for a parking spot, truly. And I’m pleased to report that the fried chicken takeaway was just as crunchy after just a few minutes in the air fryer. Hurry, put this down on your must-try list!

body:
Destination wedding costs for guests
One of your closest friends just invited you to her wedding in Bali, and you RSVP yes before you’ve even finished reading the invite. You budget for the flights and call it a day. Spoiler alert: the flights are the easy part. There’s still the hotel, the guest outfit, the angbao, and the small fortune that disappears into beach clubs and late-night Grab deliveries.
So how much does it actually cost to be a guest at a destination wedding ? We asked over a dozen people who’ve flown out for a friend or relative’s big day to tally up how much they spent, down to the last matcha latte. We also asked what happened when things didn’t go according to plan, because with a wedding, the date isn’t moving for anyone. Here’s the breakdown, plus their tips for keeping the bill in check:
Destination wedding costs at a glance
Trip length
What guests spent per person
Weekend (2-3 days)
~$570-$1,230
3-5 days
~$800-$1,200
A week or more
~$1,500-$2,800
The guests we spoke to spent anywhere from about $570 for a weekend in Malaysia where the couple covered their stay, to $2,800 for a 12-day trip in Melbourne. 7 of the 13 who flew from Singapore spent under $1,250 each.
The biggest bills, though, came from the longest trips rather than the furthest destinations. 2 guests managed weekends in Perth and Sydney for $1,100 or less.
One thing to note, all figures are per person, include gifts, and are the guests’ own estimates. So, treat them as ballpark figures rather than an exact price list.
What the table doesn’t show is how much of that money is locked in before you even leave Singapore. Flights and accommodation made up the bulk of most guests’ spending, and both are usually paid months ahead. Many of the cheapest options, like promo fares and discounted room rates, come with little to no refund if your plans change.
Take a 4-day wedding trip to Bali as an example: a $400 return flight, 3 nights at a resort for $600, a $150 outfit and a $300 angbao. That’s about $1,450, and $1,000 of it is prepaid and potentially non-refundable. It’s worth keeping track of how much you’ve committed upfront, particularly if your bookings are non-refundable or expensive to change.
Here’s where the money went:
1. Return flights: $160 to $1,200
Along with accommodation, flights took up the biggest share of most guests’ budgets. Return flights within the region cost between $160 for Malaysia and $500 for Sri Lanka, while Australia ranged from $300 for Perth to $1,200 for Melbourne.
And contrary to popular belief, distance isn’t the whole story. One guest flew to Perth for less than what another paid to get to Bali, so timing and a bit of luck matter as much as the map.
Money-saving tip: Destination wedding invites usually get sent months, and even more than a year, in advance. Book as soon as the date is confirmed and set fare alerts in the meantime. Misha, 33, locked in her flights to Kota Kinabalu 5 months ahead. She probably saved a significant amount of money as compared to those who waited till a few weekends before the trip to book a flight.
Before you pay for the cheapest fare, though, check what it costs to change it. Budget fares are often non-refundable, and change fees can cost almost as much as the ticket itself. A slightly pricier fare with free date changes can work out cheaper if there’s any chance you’ll need to move your flight. Aim to land at least a day before the ceremony too, rather than the morning of.
What if your flight gets cancelled the day before the wedding?
This is the scenario every destination wedding guest dreads. Your flight gets cancelled, or delayed so long that you’ll miss the ceremony. Unlike a regular holiday, you can’t just shift everything by a day. The wedding starts at a fixed time, with or without you.
Getting there on time usually means scrambling for the remaining seats on the next flight out, or switching airlines altogether, at last-minute prices. Depending on availability, booking a replacement flight at the last minute could cost significantly more than your original ticket, especially if you’re travelling as a family.
Image credit: Pexels
Most travel insurance plans come with a travel delay benefit, but it typically pays out based on how long you were delayed. That compensates you for the waiting, but doesn’t help you get to the wedding.
That’s the gap DirectAsia Voyager Travel Insurance ’s optional Special Events Add-On is designed to fill. If an eligible public transport disruption affects your journey to a booked special event, it can reimburse the cost of replacement public transport, plus applicable rebooking fees, so you can still get there at the next earliest time. Coverage goes up to $2,500 per insured traveller.
…
summary: We asked over a dozen Singaporeans who flew out for weddings how much they spent, from flights and villas to angbao, plus tips for keeping the bill in check.
